[113](https://fizyk20.github.io#113)// Based on work in rust-lang/rust#49000
[114](https://fizyk20.github.io#114)impl<T: Clone, N: ArrayLength> Clone for GenericArrayIter<T, N> {
[115](https://fizyk20.github.io#115)    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
[116](https://fizyk20.github.io#116)        // This places all cloned elements at the start of the new array iterator,
[117](https://fizyk20.github.io#117)        // not at their original indices.
[118](https://fizyk20.github.io#118)
[119](https://fizyk20.github.io#119)        // work from within the iter so if clone panics then the iter will drop itself.
[120](https://fizyk20.github.io#120)        let mut iter = GenericArrayIter {
[121](https://fizyk20.github.io#121)            array: unsafe { ptr::read(&self.array) },
[122](https://fizyk20.github.io#122)            index: 0,
[123](https://fizyk20.github.io#123)            index_back: 0,
[124](https://fizyk20.github.io#124)        };
[125](https://fizyk20.github.io#125)
[126](https://fizyk20.github.io#126)        for (dst, src) in iter.array.as_mut_slice().iter_mut().zip(self.as_slice()) {
[127](https://fizyk20.github.io#127)            unsafe { ptr::write(dst, src.clone()) };
[128](https://fizyk20.github.io#128)            iter.index_back += 1;
[129](https://fizyk20.github.io#129)        }
[130](https://fizyk20.github.io#130)
[131](https://fizyk20.github.io#131)        iter
[132](https://fizyk20.github.io#132)    }
[133](https://fizyk20.github.io#133)}
[134](https://fizyk20.github.io#134)
[135](https://fizyk20.github.io#135)impl<T, N: ArrayLength> Iterator for GenericArrayIter<T, N> {
[136](https://fizyk20.github.io#136)    type Item = T;
[137](https://fizyk20.github.io#137)
[138](https://fizyk20.github.io#138)    #[inline]
[139](https://fizyk20.github.io#139)    fn next(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
[140](https://fizyk20.github.io#140)        if self.index < self.index_back {
[141](https://fizyk20.github.io#141)            // SAFETY: `index < index_back <= N`, so element `index` is in bounds, alive,
[142](https://fizyk20.github.io#142)            // and not yet read. Read it by value through the base pointer (no reference to
[143](https://fizyk20.github.io#143)            // a moved-out slot is ever formed); `index` is advanced past it immediately.
[144](https://fizyk20.github.io#144)            let p = unsafe { Some(ptr::read(self.base_ptr().add(self.index))) };
[145](https://fizyk20.github.io#145)
[146](https://fizyk20.github.io#146)            self.index += 1;
[147](https://fizyk20.github.io#147)
[148](https://fizyk20.github.io#148)            p
[149](https://fizyk20.github.io#149)        } else {
[150](https://fizyk20.github.io#150)            None
[151](https://fizyk20.github.io#151)        }
[152](https://fizyk20.github.io#152)    }
[153](https://fizyk20.github.io#153)
[154](https://fizyk20.github.io#154)    #[inline]
[155](https://fizyk20.github.io#155)    fn fold<B, F>(mut self, init: B, mut f: F) -> B
[156](https://fizyk20.github.io#156)    where
[157](https://fizyk20.github.io#157)        F: FnMut(B, Self::Item) -> B,
[158](https://fizyk20.github.io#158)    {
[159](https://fizyk20.github.io#159)        let ret = unsafe {
[160](https://fizyk20.github.io#160)            let GenericArrayIter {
[161](https://fizyk20.github.io#161)                ref array,
[162](https://fizyk20.github.io#162)                ref mut index,
[163](https://fizyk20.github.io#163)                index_back,
[164](https://fizyk20.github.io#164)            } = self;
[165](https://fizyk20.github.io#165)
[166](https://fizyk20.github.io#166)            // SAFETY: `index <= index_back <= N`. Form a slice over only the live
[167](https://fizyk20.github.io#167)            // `index..index_back` range (raw cast of the array address, so no reference
[168](https://fizyk20.github.io#168)            // ever spans the moved-out slots), then read each element out by value exactly
[169](https://fizyk20.github.io#169)            // once, advancing `index` so a panic in `f` drops only the tail.
[170](https://fizyk20.github.io#170)            let remaining = &*raw_subslice!(const *array, *index, index_back);
[171](https://fizyk20.github.io#171)
[172](https://fizyk20.github.io#172)            remaining.iter().fold(init, |acc, src| {
[173](https://fizyk20.github.io#173)                let value = ptr::read(src);
[174](https://fizyk20.github.io#174)
[175](https://fizyk20.github.io#175)                *index += 1;
[176](https://fizyk20.github.io#176)
[177](https://fizyk20.github.io#177)                f(acc, value)
[178](https://fizyk20.github.io#178)            })
[179](https://fizyk20.github.io#179)        };
[180](https://fizyk20.github.io#180)
[181](https://fizyk20.github.io#181)        // The current iterator is now empty after the remaining items are
[182](https://fizyk20.github.io#182)        // consumed by the above folding. Dropping it is unnecessary,
[183](https://fizyk20.github.io#183)        // so avoid the drop codegen and forget it instead. The iterator
[184](https://fizyk20.github.io#184)        // will still drop on panics from `f`, of course.
[185](https://fizyk20.github.io#185)        //
[186](https://fizyk20.github.io#186)        // Furthermore, putting `forget` here at the end ensures the above
[187](https://fizyk20.github.io#187)        // destructuring never moves by value, so its behavior on drop remains intact.
[188](https://fizyk20.github.io#188)        mem::forget(self);
[189](https://fizyk20.github.io#189)
[190](https://fizyk20.github.io#190)        ret
[191](https://fizyk20.github.io#191)    }
[192](https://fizyk20.github.io#192)
[193](https://fizyk20.github.io#193)    #[inline(always)]
[194](https://fizyk20.github.io#194)    fn size_hint(&self) -> (usize, Option<usize>) {
[195](https://fizyk20.github.io#195)        let len = self.len();
[196](https://fizyk20.github.io#196)        (len, Some(len))
[197](https://fizyk20.github.io#197)    }
[198](https://fizyk20.github.io#198)
[199](https://fizyk20.github.io#199)    #[inline(always)]
[200](https://fizyk20.github.io#200)    fn count(self) -> usize {
[201](https://fizyk20.github.io#201)        self.len()
[202](https://fizyk20.github.io#202)    }
[203](https://fizyk20.github.io#203)
[204](https://fizyk20.github.io#204)    fn nth(&mut self, n: usize) -> Option<T> {
[205](https://fizyk20.github.io#205)        // First consume values prior to the nth.
[206](https://fizyk20.github.io#206)        let next_index = self.index + cmp::min(n, self.len());
[207](https://fizyk20.github.io#207)
[208](https://fizyk20.github.io#208)        // SAFETY: `index <= next_index <= index_back <= N`, so `index..next_index` is a
[209](https://fizyk20.github.io#209)        // range of live, in-bounds elements. Drop exactly those in place via a raw slice
[210](https://fizyk20.github.io#210)        // pointer (no reference spanning moved-out slots), then advance `index` past them.
[211](https://fizyk20.github.io#211)        unsafe {
[212](https://fizyk20.github.io#212)            ptr::drop_in_place(raw_subslice!(mut self.array, self.index, next_index));
[213](https://fizyk20.github.io#213)        }
[214](https://fizyk20.github.io#214)
[215](https://fizyk20.github.io#215)        self.index = next_index;
[216](https://fizyk20.github.io#216)
[217](https://fizyk20.github.io#217)        self.next()
[218](https://fizyk20.github.io#218)    }
[219](https://fizyk20.github.io#219)
[220](https://fizyk20.github.io#220)    #[inline]
[221](https://fizyk20.github.io#221)    fn last(mut self) -> Option<T> {
[222](https://fizyk20.github.io#222)        // Note, everything else will correctly drop first as `self` leaves scope.
[223](https://fizyk20.github.io#223)        self.next_back()
[224](https://fizyk20.github.io#224)    }

[227](https://fizyk20.github.io#227)impl<T, N: ArrayLength> DoubleEndedIterator for GenericArrayIter<T, N> {
[228](https://fizyk20.github.io#228)    #[inline]
[229](https://fizyk20.github.io#229)    fn next_back(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
[230](https://fizyk20.github.io#230)        if self.index < self.index_back {
[231](https://fizyk20.github.io#231)            self.index_back -= 1;
[232](https://fizyk20.github.io#232)
[233](https://fizyk20.github.io#233)            // SAFETY: after the decrement, `index <= index_back < N`, so element
[234](https://fizyk20.github.io#234)            // `index_back` is in bounds, alive, and not yet read. Read it by value through
[235](https://fizyk20.github.io#235)            // the base pointer; `index_back` already excludes it from the live range.
[236](https://fizyk20.github.io#236)            unsafe { Some(ptr::read(self.base_ptr().add(self.index_back))) }
[237](https://fizyk20.github.io#237)        } else {
[238](https://fizyk20.github.io#238)            None
[239](https://fizyk20.github.io#239)        }
[240](https://fizyk20.github.io#240)    }
[241](https://fizyk20.github.io#241)
[242](https://fizyk20.github.io#242)    #[inline]
[243](https://fizyk20.github.io#243)    fn rfold<B, F>(mut self, init: B, mut f: F) -> B
[244](https://fizyk20.github.io#244)    where
[245](https://fizyk20.github.io#245)        F: FnMut(B, Self::Item) -> B,
[246](https://fizyk20.github.io#246)    {
[247](https://fizyk20.github.io#247)        let ret = unsafe {
[248](https://fizyk20.github.io#248)            let GenericArrayIter {
[249](https://fizyk20.github.io#249)                ref array,
[250](https://fizyk20.github.io#250)                index,
[251](https://fizyk20.github.io#251)                ref mut index_back,
[252](https://fizyk20.github.io#252)            } = self;
[253](https://fizyk20.github.io#253)
[254](https://fizyk20.github.io#254)            // SAFETY: `index <= index_back <= N`. Form a slice over only the live
[255](https://fizyk20.github.io#255)            // `index..index_back` range (raw cast of the array address, so no reference
[256](https://fizyk20.github.io#256)            // spans moved-out slots), then read each element out by value exactly once from
[257](https://fizyk20.github.io#257)            // the back, decrementing `index_back` so a panic in `f` drops only the head.
[258](https://fizyk20.github.io#258)            let remaining = &*raw_subslice!(const *array, index, *index_back);
[259](https://fizyk20.github.io#259)
[260](https://fizyk20.github.io#260)            remaining.iter().rfold(init, |acc, src| {
[261](https://fizyk20.github.io#261)                let value = ptr::read(src);
[262](https://fizyk20.github.io#262)
[263](https://fizyk20.github.io#263)                *index_back -= 1;
[264](https://fizyk20.github.io#264)
[265](https://fizyk20.github.io#265)                f(acc, value)
[266](https://fizyk20.github.io#266)            })
[267](https://fizyk20.github.io#267)        };
[268](https://fizyk20.github.io#268)
[269](https://fizyk20.github.io#269)        // Same as `fold`
[270](https://fizyk20.github.io#270)        mem::forget(self);
[271](https://fizyk20.github.io#271)
[272](https://fizyk20.github.io#272)        ret
[273](https://fizyk20.github.io#273)    }
[274](https://fizyk20.github.io#274)
[275](https://fizyk20.github.io#275)    fn nth_back(&mut self, n: usize) -> Option<T> {
[276](https://fizyk20.github.io#276)        let next_back = self.index_back - cmp::min(n, self.len());
[277](https://fizyk20.github.io#277)
[278](https://fizyk20.github.io#278)        // SAFETY: `index <= next_back <= index_back <= N`, so `next_back..index_back` is a
[279](https://fizyk20.github.io#279)        // range of live, in-bounds elements. Drop exactly those in place via a raw slice
[280](https://fizyk20.github.io#280)        // pointer (no reference spanning moved-out slots), then retreat `index_back`.
[281](https://fizyk20.github.io#281)        unsafe {
[282](https://fizyk20.github.io#282)            ptr::drop_in_place(raw_subslice!(mut self.array, next_back, self.index_back));
[283](https://fizyk20.github.io#283)        }
[284](https://fizyk20.github.io#284)
[285](https://fizyk20.github.io#285)        self.index_back = next_back;
[286](https://fizyk20.github.io#286)
[287](https://fizyk20.github.io#287)        self.next_back()
[288](https://fizyk20.github.io#288)    }

# Serialize in serde_core::ser - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/serde_core/ser/trait.Serialize.html

```
pub trait Serialize {
    // Required method
    fn
```
[serialize](https://fizyk20.github.io#tymethod.serialize)<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<S::[Ok](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Ok), S::[Error](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>
       where S: [Serializer](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Serializer.html);
}## Expand description

A **data structure** that can be serialized into any data format supported
by Serde.

Serde provides `Serialize` implementations for many Rust primitive and
standard library types. The complete list is [here](https://fizyk20.github.io/index.html). All of
these can be serialized using Serde out of the box.

Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [ serde_derive](https://crates.io/crates/serde_derive) to
automatically generate

`Serialize` implementations for structs and enums in
your program. See the [derive section of the manual](https://serde.rs/derive.html)for how to use this.

In rare cases it may be necessary to implement `Serialize` manually for some
type in your program. See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the
manual for more about this.

Third-party crates may provide `Serialize` implementations for types that
they expose. For example the [ linked-hash-map](https://crates.io/crates/linked-hash-map) crate provides a

[type that is serializable by Serde because the crate provides an implementation of](https://docs.rs/linked-hash-map/*/linked_hash_map/struct.LinkedHashMap.html)

`LinkedHashMap<K, V>``Serialize` for it.## Required Methods[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#required-methods)

Serialize this value into the given Serde serializer.

See the [Implementing  Serialize](https://serde.rs/impl-serialize.html) section of the manual for more
information about how to implement this method.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
// This is what #[derive(Serialize)] would generate.
impl Serialize for Person {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut s = serializer.serialize_struct("Person", 3)?;
        s.serialize_field("name", &self.name)?;
        s.serialize_field("age", &self.age)?;
        s.serialize_field("phones", &self.phones)?;
        s.end()
    }
}
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

## Implementations on Foreign Types[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#foreign-impls)

[Source](https://fizyk20.github.io/src/serde_core/ser/impls.rs.html#397-402)[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#impl-Serialize-for-(T,))### impl<T> [Serialize](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Serialize.html) for [(T₁, T₂, …, Tₙ)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.tuple.html#trait-implementations-1)

This trait is implemented for tuples up to 16 items long.

}## Expand description

A **data format** that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

The role of this trait is to define the serialization half of the [Serde
data model](https://serde.rs/data-model.html), which is a way to categorize every Rust data structure into one
of 29 possible types. Each method of the `Serializer` trait corresponds to
one of the types of the data model.

Implementations of `Serialize` map themselves into this data model by
invoking exactly one of the `Serializer` methods.

The types that make up the Serde data model are:

- **14 primitive types**- bool
- i8, i16, i32, i64, i128
- u8, u16, u32, u64, u128
- f32, f64
- char

- **string**- UTF-8 bytes with a length and no null terminator.
- When serializing, all strings are handled equally. When deserializing, there are three flavors of strings: transient, owned, and borrowed.

- **byte array**- [u8]- Similar to strings, during deserialization byte arrays can be transient, owned, or borrowed.

- **option**- Either none or some value.

- **unit**- The type of `()`in Rust. It represents an anonymous value containing no data.

- The type of
- **unit_struct**- For example `struct Unit`or`PhantomData<T>`. It represents a named value containing no data.

- For example
- **unit_variant**- For example the `E::A`and`E::B`in`enum E { A, B }`.

- For example the
- **newtype_struct**- For example `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

- For example
- **newtype_variant**- For example the `E::N`in`enum E { N(u8) }`.

- For example the
- **seq**- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
`Vec<T>`or`HashSet<T>`. When serializing, the length may or may not be known before iterating through all the data. When deserializing, the length is determined by looking at the serialized data.

- A variably sized heterogeneous sequence of values, for example
- **tuple**- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `(u8,)`or`(String, u64, Vec<T>)`or`[u64; 10]`.

- A statically sized heterogeneous sequence of values for which the
length will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **tuple_struct**- A named tuple, for example `struct Rgb(u8, u8, u8)`.

- A named tuple, for example
- **tuple_variant**- For example the `E::T`in`enum E { T(u8, u8) }`.

- For example the
- **map**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example `BTreeMap<K, V>`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing, for example
- **struct**- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example `struct S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.

- A heterogeneous key-value pairing in which the keys are strings and
will be known at deserialization time without looking at the
serialized data, for example
- **struct_variant**- For example the `E::S`in`enum E { S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 } }`.

- For example the

Many Serde serializers produce text or binary data as output, for example
JSON or Postcard. This is not a requirement of the `Serializer` trait, and
there are serializers that do not produce text or binary output. One example
is the `serde_json::value::Serializer` (distinct from the main `serde_json`
serializer) that produces a `serde_json::Value` data structure in memory as
output.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#example-implementation)Example implementation

The [example data format](https://serde.rs/data-format.html) presented on the website contains example code for
a basic JSON `Serializer`.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#required-associated-types)

The output type produced by this `Serializer` during successful
serialization. Most serializers that produce text or binary output
should set `Ok = ()` and serialize into an [ io::Write](std::io::Write) or buffer
contained within the

`Serializer` instance. Serializers that build
in-memory data structures may be simplified by using `Ok` to propagate

Serialize an `i8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i8` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i16` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize an `i32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `i32` and `i64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `i64` and
forward to `serialize_i64`.

Serialize a `u8` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u8` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u16` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u16` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize a `u32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `u32` and `u64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `u64` and
forward to `serialize_u64`.

Serialize an `f32` value.

If the format does not differentiate between `f32` and `f64`, a
reasonable implementation would be to cast the value to `f64` and
forward to `serialize_f64`.

Serialize a character.

If the format does not support characters, it is reasonable to serialize
it as a single element `str` or a `u32`.

Serialize a chunk of raw byte data.

Enables serializers to serialize byte slices more compactly or more
efficiently than other types of slices. If no efficient implementation
is available, a reasonable implementation would be to forward to
`serialize_seq`. If forwarded, the implementation looks usually just
like this:

Serialize a unit struct like `struct Unit` or `PhantomData<T>`.

A reasonable implementation would be to forward to `serialize_unit`.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Nothing;
impl Serialize for Nothing {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.serialize_unit_struct("Nothing")
    }
}
```

Serialize a unit variant like `E::A` in `enum E { A, B }`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, and the `variant` is the name of the
variant.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
enum E {
    A,
    B,
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::A => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 0, "A"),
            E::B => serializer.serialize_unit_variant("E", 1, "B"),
        }
    }
}
```

Serialize a newtype struct like `struct Millimeters(u8)`.

Serializers are encouraged to treat newtype structs as insignificant
wrappers around the data they contain. A reasonable implementation would
be to forward to `value.serialize(self)`.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
struct Millimeters(u8);
impl Serialize for Millimeters {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.serialize_newtype_struct("Millimeters", &self.0)
    }
}
```

[Source](https://fizyk20.github.io/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#950-958)

Serialize a newtype variant like `E::N` in `enum E { N(u8) }`.

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, and the `variant` is the name of the
variant. The `value` is the data contained within this newtype variant.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
enum E {
    M(String),
    N(u8),
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::M(ref s) => serializer.serialize_newtype_variant("E", 0, "M", s),
            E::N(n) => serializer.serialize_newtype_variant("E", 1, "N", &n),
        }
    }
}

#### fn [serialize_seq](https://fizyk20.github.io#tymethod.serialize_seq)(
    self,
    len: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html)>,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeSeq](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeSeq), Self::[Error](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Begin to serialize a variably sized sequence. This call must be
followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`, then a call to
`end`.

The argument is the number of elements in the sequence, which may or may not be computable before the sequence is iterated. Some serializers only support sequences whose length is known up front.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeSeq, Serializer};
impl<T> Serialize for Vec<T>
where
    T: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut seq = serializer.serialize_seq(Some(self.len()))?;
        for element in self {
            seq.serialize_element(element)?;
        }
        seq.end()
    }
}
```

Begin to serialize a statically sized sequence whose length will be
known at deserialization time without looking at the serialized data.
This call must be followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_element`,
then a call to `end`.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTuple, Serializer};
impl<A, B, C> Serialize for (A, B, C)
where
    A: Serialize,
    B: Serialize,
    C: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut tup = serializer.serialize_tuple(3)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.0)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.1)?;
        tup.serialize_element(&self.2)?;
        tup.end()
    }
}
```
[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTuple, Serializer};
const VRAM_SIZE: usize = 386;
struct Vram([u16; VRAM_SIZE]);
impl Serialize for Vram {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut seq = serializer.serialize_tuple(VRAM_SIZE)?;
        for element in &self.0[..] {
            seq.serialize_element(element)?;
        }
        seq.end()
    }
}
```

The `name` is the name of the enum, the `variant_index` is the index of
this variant within the enum, the `variant` is the name of the variant,
and the `len` is the number of data fields that will be serialized.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeTupleVariant, Serializer};
enum E {
    T(u8, u8),
    U(String, u32, u32),
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::T(ref a, ref b) => {
                let mut tv = serializer.serialize_tuple_variant("E", 0, "T", 2)?;
                tv.serialize_field(a)?;
                tv.serialize_field(b)?;
                tv.end()
            }
            E::U(ref a, ref b, ref c) => {
                let mut tv = serializer.serialize_tuple_variant("E", 1, "U", 3)?;
                tv.serialize_field(a)?;
                tv.serialize_field(b)?;
                tv.serialize_field(c)?;
                tv.end()
            }
        }
    }
}
```

#### fn [serialize_map](https://fizyk20.github.io#tymethod.serialize_map)(
    self,
    len: [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html)>,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[SerializeMap](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.SerializeMap), Self::[Error](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Serializer.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Begin to serialize a map. This call must be followed by zero or more
calls to `serialize_key` and `serialize_value`, then a call to `end`.

The argument is the number of elements in the map, which may or may not be computable before the map is iterated. Some serializers only support maps whose length is known up front.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeMap, Serializer};
impl<K, V> Serialize for HashMap<K, V>
where
    K: Serialize,
    V: Serialize,
{
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut map = serializer.serialize_map(Some(self.len()))?;
        for (k, v) in self {
            map.serialize_entry(k, v)?;
        }
        map.end()
    }
}
```

#### fn [serialize_struct](https://fizyk20.github.io#tymethod.serialize_struct)(

Begin to serialize a struct like `struct Rgb { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 }`.
This call must be followed by zero or more calls to `serialize_field`,
then a call to `end`.

The `name` is the name of the struct and the `len` is the number of
data fields that will be serialized. `len` does not include fields
which are skipped with [ SerializeStruct::skip_field](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.SerializeStruct.html#method.skip_field).

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStruct, Serializer};
struct Rgb {
    r: u8,
    g: u8,
    b: u8,
}
impl Serialize for Rgb {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        let mut rgb = serializer.serialize_struct("Rgb", 3)?;
        rgb.serialize_field("r", &self.r)?;
        rgb.serialize_field("g", &self.g)?;
        rgb.serialize_field("b", &self.b)?;
        rgb.end()
    }
}
```

use serde::ser::{Serialize, SerializeStructVariant, Serializer};

    S { r: u8, g: u8, b: u8 },
}
impl Serialize for E {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        match *self {
            E::S {
                ref r,
                ref g,
                ref b,
            } => {
                let mut sv = serializer.serialize_struct_variant("E", 0, "S", 3)?;
                sv.serialize_field("r", r)?;

                sv.serialize_field("b", b)?;

`alloc` nor crate feature `std`Serialize a string produced by an implementation of `Display`.

Serializers that use `no_std` are required to provide an implementation
of this method. If no more sensible behavior is possible, the
implementation is expected to return an error.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
impl Serialize for DateTime {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_str(&format_args!("{:?}{:?}", self.naive_local(), self.offset()))
    }
}

    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_seq(self.data.iter().map(|x| x + 1))
    }
}

    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        serializer.collect_map(self.keys.iter().map(|k| (k, ())))

[Source](https://fizyk20.github.io/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#1459-1461)#### fn [is_human_readable](https://fizyk20.github.io#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://fizyk20.github.io/src/serde_core/ser/mod.rs.html#1459-1461)

#### fn [is_human_readable](https://fizyk20.github.io#method.is_human_readable)(&self) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html)

Determine whether `Serialize` implementations should serialize in
human-readable form.

Some types have a human-readable form that may be somewhat expensive to construct, as well as a binary form that is compact and efficient. Generally text-based formats like JSON and YAML will prefer to use the human-readable one and binary formats like Postcard will prefer the compact one.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use serde::{Serialize, Serializer};
impl Serialize for Timestamp {
    fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
    where
        S: Serializer,
    {
        if serializer.is_human_readable() {
            // Serialize to a human-readable string "2015-05-15T17:01:00Z".
            self.to_string().serialize(serializer)
        } else {
            // Serialize to a compact binary representation.
            self.seconds_since_epoch().serialize(serializer)
        }
    }
}
```
The default implementation of this method returns `true`. Data formats
may override this to `false` to request a compact form for types that
support one. Note that modifying this method to change a format from
human-readable to compact or vice versa should be regarded as a breaking
change, as a value serialized in human-readable mode is not required to
deserialize from the same data in compact mode.

# anybitpattern.rs - source

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/src/bytemuck/anybitpattern.rs.html

# bytemuck/anybitpattern.rs

[1](https://fizyk20.github.io#1)use crate::{Pod, Zeroable};
[2](https://fizyk20.github.io#2)
[3](https://fizyk20.github.io#3)/// Marker trait for "plain old data" types that are valid for any bit pattern.
[4](https://fizyk20.github.io#4)///
[5](https://fizyk20.github.io#5)/// The requirements for this is very similar to [`Pod`], except that the type
[6](https://fizyk20.github.io#6)/// can allow uninit (or padding) bytes. This limits what you can do with a type
[7](https://fizyk20.github.io#7)/// of this kind, but also broadens the included types to `repr(C)` `struct`s
[8](https://fizyk20.github.io#8)/// that contain padding as well as `union`s. Notably, you can only cast
[9](https://fizyk20.github.io#9)/// *immutable* references and *owned* values into [`AnyBitPattern`] types, not
[10](https://fizyk20.github.io#10)/// *mutable* references.
[11](https://fizyk20.github.io#11)///
[12](https://fizyk20.github.io#12)/// [`Pod`] is a subset of [`AnyBitPattern`], meaning that any `T: Pod` is also
[13](https://fizyk20.github.io#13)/// [`AnyBitPattern`] but any `T: AnyBitPattern` is not necessarily [`Pod`].
[14](https://fizyk20.github.io#14)///
[15](https://fizyk20.github.io#15)/// [`AnyBitPattern`] is a subset of [`Zeroable`], meaning that any `T:
[16](https://fizyk20.github.io#16)/// AnyBitPattern` is also [`Zeroable`], but any `T: Zeroable` is not
[17](https://fizyk20.github.io#17)/// necessarily [`AnyBitPattern`]
[18](https://fizyk20.github.io#18)///
[19](https://fizyk20.github.io#19)/// # Derive
[20](https://fizyk20.github.io#20)///
[21](https://fizyk20.github.io#21)/// A `#[derive(AnyBitPattern)]` macro is provided under the `derive` feature
[22](https://fizyk20.github.io#22)/// flag which will automatically validate the requirements of this trait and
[23](https://fizyk20.github.io#23)/// implement the trait for you for both structs and enums. This is the
[24](https://fizyk20.github.io#24)/// recommended method for implementing the trait, however it's also possible to
[25](https://fizyk20.github.io#25)/// do manually. If you implement it manually, you *must* carefully follow the
[26](https://fizyk20.github.io#26)/// below safety rules.
[27](https://fizyk20.github.io#27)///
[28](https://fizyk20.github.io#28)/// * *NOTE: even `C-style`, fieldless enums are intentionally **excluded** from
[29](https://fizyk20.github.io#29)///   this trait, since it is **unsound** for an enum to have a discriminant
[30](https://fizyk20.github.io#30)///   value that is not one of its defined variants.
[31](https://fizyk20.github.io#31)///
[32](https://fizyk20.github.io#32)/// # Safety
[33](https://fizyk20.github.io#33)///
[34](https://fizyk20.github.io#34)/// Similar to [`Pod`] except we disregard the rule about it must not contain
[35](https://fizyk20.github.io#35)/// uninit bytes. Still, this is a quite strong guarantee about a type, so *be
[36](https://fizyk20.github.io#36)/// careful* when implementing it manually.
[37](https://fizyk20.github.io#37)///
[38](https://fizyk20.github.io#38)/// * The type must be inhabited (eg: no
[39](https://fizyk20.github.io#39)///   [Infallible](core::convert::Infallible)).
[40](https://fizyk20.github.io#40)/// * The type must be valid for any bit pattern of its backing memory.
[41](https://fizyk20.github.io#41)/// * Structs need to have all fields also be `AnyBitPattern`.
[42](https://fizyk20.github.io#42)/// * It is disallowed for types to contain pointer types, `Cell`, `UnsafeCell`,
[43](https://fizyk20.github.io#43)///   atomics, and any other forms of interior mutability.
[44](https://fizyk20.github.io#44)/// * More precisely: A shared reference to the type must allow reads, and
[45](https://fizyk20.github.io#45)///   *only* reads. RustBelt's separation logic is based on the notion that a
[46](https://fizyk20.github.io#46)///   type is allowed to define a sharing predicate, its own invariant that must
[47](https://fizyk20.github.io#47)///   hold for shared references, and this predicate is the reasoning that allow
[48](https://fizyk20.github.io#48)///   it to deal with atomic and cells etc. We require the sharing predicate to
[49](https://fizyk20.github.io#49)///   be trivial and permit only read-only access.
[50](https://fizyk20.github.io#50)/// * There's probably more, don't mess it up (I mean it).
[51](https://fizyk20.github.io#51)pub unsafe trait AnyBitPattern:
[52](https://fizyk20.github.io#52)  Zeroable + Sized + Copy + 'static
[53](https://fizyk20.github.io#53){
[54](https://fizyk20.github.io#54)}
[55](https://fizyk20.github.io#55)
[56](https://fizyk20.github.io#56)unsafe impl<T: Pod> AnyBitPattern for T {}
[57](https://fizyk20.github.io#57)
[58](https://fizyk20.github.io#58)#[cfg(feature = "zeroable_maybe_uninit")]
[59](https://fizyk20.github.io#59)#[cfg_attr(
[60](https://fizyk20.github.io#60)  feature = "nightly_docs",
[61](https://fizyk20.github.io#61)  doc(cfg(feature = "zeroable_maybe_uninit"))

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#immutable-bit-view)Immutable Bit View

This trait is an analogue to the [ AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html) trait, in that it enables any type to
provide a view of an immutable bit-slice.

It does not require an `AsRef<[T: BitStore]>` implementation, but a blanket
implementation for all `AsRef<[T: BitStore]>` is provided. This allows you to
choose whether to implement only one of `AsBits<T>` or `AsRef<[T]>`, and gain
a bit-slice view through either choice.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#usage)Usage

The `.as_bits<_>()` method has the same usage patterns as
[ BitView::view_bits](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.BitView.html#tymethod.view_bits).

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#notes)Notes

You are not *forbidden* from creating multiple views with different element
types to the same region, but doing so is likely to cause inconsistent and
surprising behavior.

Refrain from implementing this trait with more than one storage argument unless you are sure that you can uphold the memory region requirements of all of them, and are aware of the behavior conflicts that may arise.

## Required Methods[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#required-methods)

Views `self` as an immutable bit-slice region with the `O` ordering.

# checked.rs - source

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/src/bytemuck/checked.rs.html

# bytemuck/checked.rs

[1](https://fizyk20.github.io#1)//! Checked versions of the casting functions exposed in crate root
[2](https://fizyk20.github.io#2)//! that support [`CheckedBitPattern`] types.
[3](https://fizyk20.github.io#3)
[4](https://fizyk20.github.io#4)use crate::{
[5](https://fizyk20.github.io#5)  internal::{self, something_went_wrong},
[6](https://fizyk20.github.io#6)  AnyBitPattern, NoUninit,
[7](https://fizyk20.github.io#7)};
[8](https://fizyk20.github.io#8)
[9](https://fizyk20.github.io#9)/// A marker trait that allows types that have some invalid bit patterns to be
[10](https://fizyk20.github.io#10)/// used in places that otherwise require [`AnyBitPattern`] or [`Pod`] types by
[11](https://fizyk20.github.io#11)/// performing a runtime check on a perticular set of bits. This is particularly
[12](https://fizyk20.github.io#12)/// useful for types like fieldless ('C-style') enums, [`char`], bool, and
[13](https://fizyk20.github.io#13)/// structs containing them.
[14](https://fizyk20.github.io#14)///
[15](https://fizyk20.github.io#15)/// To do this, we define a `Bits` type which is a type with equivalent layout
[16](https://fizyk20.github.io#16)/// to `Self` other than the invalid bit patterns which disallow `Self` from
[17](https://fizyk20.github.io#17)/// being [`AnyBitPattern`]. This `Bits` type must itself implement
[18](https://fizyk20.github.io#18)/// [`AnyBitPattern`]. Then, we implement a function that checks whether a
[19](https://fizyk20.github.io#19)/// certain instance of the `Bits` is also a valid bit pattern of `Self`. If
[20](https://fizyk20.github.io#20)/// this check passes, then we can allow casting from the `Bits` to `Self` (and
[21](https://fizyk20.github.io#21)/// therefore, any type which is able to be cast to `Bits` is also able to be
[22](https://fizyk20.github.io#22)/// cast to `Self`).
[23](https://fizyk20.github.io#23)///
[24](https://fizyk20.github.io#24)/// [`AnyBitPattern`] is a subset of [`CheckedBitPattern`], meaning that any `T:
[25](https://fizyk20.github.io#25)/// AnyBitPattern` is also [`CheckedBitPattern`]. This means you can also use
[26](https://fizyk20.github.io#26)/// any [`AnyBitPattern`] type in the checked versions of casting functions in
[27](https://fizyk20.github.io#27)/// this module. If it's possible, prefer implementing [`AnyBitPattern`] for
[28](https://fizyk20.github.io#28)/// your type directly instead of [`CheckedBitPattern`] as it gives greater
[29](https://fizyk20.github.io#29)/// flexibility.
[30](https://fizyk20.github.io#30)///
[31](https://fizyk20.github.io#31)/// # Derive
[32](https://fizyk20.github.io#32)///
[33](https://fizyk20.github.io#33)/// A `#[derive(CheckedBitPattern)]` macro is provided under the `derive`
[34](https://fizyk20.github.io#34)/// feature flag which will automatically validate the requirements of this
[35](https://fizyk20.github.io#35)/// trait and implement the trait for you for both enums and structs. This is
[36](https://fizyk20.github.io#36)/// the recommended method for implementing the trait, however it's also
[37](https://fizyk20.github.io#37)/// possible to do manually.
[38](https://fizyk20.github.io#38)///
[39](https://fizyk20.github.io#39)/// # Example
[40](https://fizyk20.github.io#40)///
[41](https://fizyk20.github.io#41)/// If manually implementing the trait, we can do something like so:
[42](https://fizyk20.github.io#42)///
[43](https://fizyk20.github.io#43)/// ```rust
[44](https://fizyk20.github.io#44)/// use bytemuck::{CheckedBitPattern, NoUninit};
[45](https://fizyk20.github.io#45)///
[46](https://fizyk20.github.io#46)/// #[repr(u32)]
[47](https://fizyk20.github.io#47)/// #[derive(Copy, Clone)]
[48](https://fizyk20.github.io#48)/// enum MyEnum {
[49](https://fizyk20.github.io#49)///     Variant0 = 0,
[50](https://fizyk20.github.io#50)///     Variant1 = 1,
[51](https://fizyk20.github.io#51)///     Variant2 = 2,
[52](https://fizyk20.github.io#52)/// }
[53](https://fizyk20.github.io#53)///
[54](https://fizyk20.github.io#54)/// unsafe impl CheckedBitPattern for MyEnum {
[55](https://fizyk20.github.io#55)///     type Bits = u32;
[56](https://fizyk20.github.io#56)///
[57](https://fizyk20.github.io#57)///     fn is_valid_bit_pattern(bits: &u32) -> bool {
[58](https://fizyk20.github.io#58)///         match *bits {
[59](https://fizyk20.github.io#59)///             0 | 1 | 2 => true,
[60](https://fizyk20.github.io#60)///             _ => false,
[61](https://fizyk20.github.io#61)///         }
[62](https://fizyk20.github.io#62)///     }
[63](https://fizyk20.github.io#63)/// }
[64](https://fizyk20.github.io#64)///
[65](https://fizyk20.github.io#65)/// // It is often useful to also implement `NoUninit` on our `CheckedBitPattern` types.
[66](https://fizyk20.github.io#66)/// // This will allow us to do casting of mutable references (and mutable slices).
[67](https://fizyk20.github.io#67)/// // It is not always possible to do so, but in this case we have no padding so it is.
[68](https://fizyk20.github.io#68)/// unsafe impl NoUninit for MyEnum {}
[69](https://fizyk20.github.io#69)/// ```
[70](https://fizyk20.github.io#70)///
[71](https://fizyk20.github.io#71)/// We can now use relevant casting functions. For example,
[72](https://fizyk20.github.io#72)///
[73](https://fizyk20.github.io#73)/// ```rust
[74](https://fizyk20.github.io#74)/// # use bytemuck::{CheckedBitPattern, NoUninit};
[75](https://fizyk20.github.io#75)/// # #[repr(u32)]
[76](https://fizyk20.github.io#76)/// # #[derive(Copy, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Debug)]
[77](https://fizyk20.github.io#77)/// # enum MyEnum {
[78](https://fizyk20.github.io#78)/// #     Variant0 = 0,
[79](https://fizyk20.github.io#79)/// #     Variant1 = 1,
[80](https://fizyk20.github.io#80)/// #     Variant2 = 2,
[81](https://fizyk20.github.io#81)/// # }
[82](https://fizyk20.github.io#82)/// # unsafe impl NoUninit for MyEnum {}
[83](https://fizyk20.github.io#83)/// # unsafe impl CheckedBitPattern for MyEnum {
[84](https://fizyk20.github.io#84)/// #     type Bits = u32;
[85](https://fizyk20.github.io#85)/// #     fn is_valid_bit_pattern(bits: &u32) -> bool {
[86](https://fizyk20.github.io#86)/// #         match *bits {
[87](https://fizyk20.github.io#87)/// #             0 | 1 | 2 => true,
[88](https://fizyk20.github.io#88)/// #             _ => false,
[89](https://fizyk20.github.io#89)/// #         }
[90](https://fizyk20.github.io#90)/// #     }
[91](https://fizyk20.github.io#91)/// # }
[92](https://fizyk20.github.io#92)/// use bytemuck::{bytes_of, bytes_of_mut};
[93](https://fizyk20.github.io#93)/// use bytemuck::checked;
[94](https://fizyk20.github.io#94)///
[95](https://fizyk20.github.io#95)/// let bytes = bytes_of(&2u32);
[96](https://fizyk20.github.io#96)/// let result = checked::try_from_bytes::<MyEnum>(bytes);
[97](https://fizyk20.github.io#97)/// assert_eq!(result, Ok(&MyEnum::Variant2));
[98](https://fizyk20.github.io#98)///
[99](https://fizyk20.github.io#99)/// // Fails for invalid discriminant
[100](https://fizyk20.github.io#100)/// let bytes = bytes_of(&100u32);
[101](https://fizyk20.github.io#101)/// let result = checked::try_from_bytes::<MyEnum>(bytes);
[102](https://fizyk20.github.io#102)/// assert!(result.is_err());
[103](https://fizyk20.github.io#103)///
[104](https://fizyk20.github.io#104)/// // Since we implemented NoUninit, we can also cast mutably from an original type
[105](https://fizyk20.github.io#105)/// // that is `NoUninit + AnyBitPattern`:
[106](https://fizyk20.github.io#106)/// let mut my_u32 = 2u32;
[107](https://fizyk20.github.io#107)/// {
[108](https://fizyk20.github.io#108)///   let as_enum_mut = checked::cast_mut::<_, MyEnum>(&mut my_u32);
[109](https://fizyk20.github.io#109)///   assert_eq!(as_enum_mut, &mut MyEnum::Variant2);
[110](https://fizyk20.github.io#110)///   *as_enum_mut = MyEnum::Variant0;
[111](https://fizyk20.github.io#111)/// }
[112](https://fizyk20.github.io#112)/// assert_eq!(my_u32, 0u32);
[113](https://fizyk20.github.io#113)/// ```
[114](https://fizyk20.github.io#114)///
[115](https://fizyk20.github.io#115)/// # Safety
[116](https://fizyk20.github.io#116)///
[117](https://fizyk20.github.io#117)/// * `Self` *must* have the same layout as the specified `Bits` except for the
[118](https://fizyk20.github.io#118)///   possible invalid bit patterns being checked during
[119](https://fizyk20.github.io#119)///   [`is_valid_bit_pattern`].
[120](https://fizyk20.github.io#120)/// * This almost certainly means your type must be `#[repr(C)]` or a similar
[121](https://fizyk20.github.io#121)///   specified repr, but if you think you know better, you probably don't. If
[122](https://fizyk20.github.io#122)///   you still think you know better, be careful and have fun. And don't mess
[123](https://fizyk20.github.io#123)///   it up (I mean it).
[124](https://fizyk20.github.io#124)/// * If [`is_valid_bit_pattern`] returns true, then the bit pattern contained
[125](https://fizyk20.github.io#125)///   in `bits` must also be valid for an instance of `Self`.
[126](https://fizyk20.github.io#126)/// * Probably more, don't mess it up (I mean it 2.0)
[127](https://fizyk20.github.io#127)///
[128](https://fizyk20.github.io#128)/// [`is_valid_bit_pattern`]: CheckedBitPattern::is_valid_bit_pattern
[129](https://fizyk20.github.io#129)/// [`Pod`]: crate::Pod

[241](https://fizyk20.github.io#241)/// Re-interprets `&[u8]` as `&T`.
[242](https://fizyk20.github.io#242)///
[243](https://fizyk20.github.io#243)/// ## Failure
[244](https://fizyk20.github.io#244)///
[245](https://fizyk20.github.io#245)/// * If the slice isn't aligned for the new type
[246](https://fizyk20.github.io#246)/// * If the slice's length isn’t exactly the size of the new type
[247](https://fizyk20.github.io#247)/// * If the slice contains an invalid bit pattern for `T`

[249](https://fizyk20.github.io#249)pub fn try_from_bytes<T: CheckedBitPattern>(
[250](https://fizyk20.github.io#250)  s: &[u8],
[251](https://fizyk20.github.io#251)) -> Result<&T, CheckedCastError> {
[252](https://fizyk20.github.io#252)  let pod = crate::try_from_bytes(s)?;
[253](https://fizyk20.github.io#253)
[254](https://fizyk20.github.io#254)  if <T as CheckedBitPattern>::is_valid_bit_pattern(pod) {
[255](https://fizyk20.github.io#255)    Ok(unsafe { &*(pod as *const <T as CheckedBitPattern>::Bits as *const T) })
[256](https://fizyk20.github.io#256)  } else {
[257](https://fizyk20.github.io#257)    Err(CheckedCastError::InvalidBitPattern)
[258](https://fizyk20.github.io#258)  }

[362](https://fizyk20.github.io#362)/// Try to convert `&[A]` into `&[B]` (possibly with a change in length).
[363](https://fizyk20.github.io#363)///
[364](https://fizyk20.github.io#364)/// * `input.as_ptr() as usize == output.as_ptr() as usize`
[365](https://fizyk20.github.io#365)/// * `input.len() * size_of::<A>() == output.len() * size_of::<B>()`
[366](https://fizyk20.github.io#366)///
[367](https://fizyk20.github.io#367)/// ## Failure
[368](https://fizyk20.github.io#368)///
[369](https://fizyk20.github.io#369)/// * If the target type has a greater alignment requirement and the input slice
[370](https://fizyk20.github.io#370)///   isn't aligned.
[371](https://fizyk20.github.io#371)/// * If the target element type is a different size from the current element
[372](https://fizyk20.github.io#372)///   type, and the output slice wouldn't be a whole number of elements when
[373](https://fizyk20.github.io#373)///   accounting for the size change (eg: 3 `u16` values is 1.5 `u32` values, so
[374](https://fizyk20.github.io#374)///   that's a failure).
[375](https://fizyk20.github.io#375)/// * If any element of the converted slice would contain an invalid bit pattern
[376](https://fizyk20.github.io#376)///   for `B` this fails.
[377](https://fizyk20.github.io#377)#[inline]
[378](https://fizyk20.github.io#378)pub fn try_cast_slice<A: NoUninit, B: CheckedBitPattern>(
[379](https://fizyk20.github.io#379)  a: &[A],
[380](https://fizyk20.github.io#380)) -> Result<&[B], CheckedCastError> {
[381](https://fizyk20.github.io#381)  let pod = crate::try_cast_slice(a)?;
[382](https://fizyk20.github.io#382)
[383](https://fizyk20.github.io#383)  if pod.iter().all(|pod| <B as CheckedBitPattern>::is_valid_bit_pattern(pod)) {
[384](https://fizyk20.github.io#384)    Ok(unsafe {
[385](https://fizyk20.github.io#385)      core::slice::from_raw_parts(pod.as_ptr() as *const B, pod.len())
[386](https://fizyk20.github.io#386)    })
[387](https://fizyk20.github.io#387)  } else {
[388](https://fizyk20.github.io#388)    Err(CheckedCastError::InvalidBitPattern)
[389](https://fizyk20.github.io#389)  }
[390](https://fizyk20.github.io#390)}
[391](https://fizyk20.github.io#391)

# CheckedBitPattern in bytemuck::checked - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/bytemuck/checked/trait.CheckedBitPattern.html

`pub unsafe trait CheckedBitPattern: `[Copy](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Copy.html) {
    type [Bits](https://fizyk20.github.io#associatedtype.Bits): [AnyBitPattern](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.AnyBitPattern.html);
    // Required method
    fn [is_valid_bit_pattern](https://fizyk20.github.io#tymethod.is_valid_bit_pattern)(bits: &Self::[Bits](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.CheckedBitPattern.html#associatedtype.Bits)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.bool.html);
}## Expand description

A marker trait that allows types that have some invalid bit patterns to be
used in places that otherwise require [ AnyBitPattern](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.AnyBitPattern.html) or

[types by performing a runtime check on a perticular set of bits. This is particularly useful for types like fieldless (‘C-style’) enums,](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Pod.html)

`Pod`[, bool, and structs containing them.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.char.html)

`char`To do this, we define a `Bits` type which is a type with equivalent layout
to `Self` other than the invalid bit patterns which disallow `Self` from
being [ AnyBitPattern](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.AnyBitPattern.html). This

`Bits` type must itself implement
[. Then, we implement a function that checks whether a certain instance of the](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern``Bits` is also a valid bit pattern of `Self`. If
this check passes, then we can allow casting from the `Bits` to `Self` (and
therefore, any type which is able to be cast to `Bits` is also able to be
cast to `Self`).[ AnyBitPattern](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.AnyBitPattern.html) is a subset of

[, meaning that any](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.CheckedBitPattern.html)

`CheckedBitPattern``T: AnyBitPattern` is also [. This means you can also use any](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.CheckedBitPattern.html)

`CheckedBitPattern`[type in the checked versions of casting functions in this module. If it’s possible, prefer implementing](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`[for your type directly instead of](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`[as it gives greater flexibility.](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.CheckedBitPattern.html)

`CheckedBitPattern`[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#derive)Derive

A `#[derive(CheckedBitPattern)]` macro is provided under the `derive`
feature flag which will automatically validate the requirements of this
trait and implement the trait for you for both enums and structs. This is
the recommended method for implementing the trait, however it’s also
possible to do manually.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#example)Example

If manually implementing the trait, we can do something like so:

```
use bytemuck::{CheckedBitPattern, NoUninit};
#[repr(u32)]
#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
enum MyEnum {
    Variant0 = 0,
    Variant1 = 1,
    Variant2 = 2,
}
unsafe impl CheckedBitPattern for MyEnum {
    type Bits = u32;
    fn is_valid_bit_pattern(bits: &u32) -> bool {
        match *bits {
            0 | 1 | 2 => true,
            _ => false,
        }
    }
}
// It is often useful to also implement `NoUninit` on our `CheckedBitPattern` types.
// This will allow us to do casting of mutable references (and mutable slices).
// It is not always possible to do so, but in this case we have no padding so it is.
unsafe impl NoUninit for MyEnum {}
```
We can now use relevant casting functions. For example,

```
use bytemuck::{bytes_of, bytes_of_mut};
use bytemuck::checked;
let bytes = bytes_of(&2u32);
let result = checked::try_from_bytes::<MyEnum>(bytes);
assert_eq!(result, Ok(&MyEnum::Variant2));
// Fails for invalid discriminant
let bytes = bytes_of(&100u32);
let result = checked::try_from_bytes::<MyEnum>(bytes);
assert!(result.is_err());
// Since we implemented NoUninit, we can also cast mutably from an original type
// that is `NoUninit + AnyBitPattern`:
let mut my_u32 = 2u32;
{
  let as_enum_mut = checked::cast_mut::<_, MyEnum>(&mut my_u32);
  assert_eq!(as_enum_mut, &mut MyEnum::Variant2);
  *as_enum_mut = MyEnum::Variant0;
}
assert_eq!(my_u32, 0u32);
```
[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#safety)Safety

- `Self`- *must*have the same layout as the specified- `Bits`except for the possible invalid bit patterns being checked during- `is_valid_bit_pattern`
- This almost certainly means your type must be `#[repr(C)]`or a similar specified repr, but if you think you know better, you probably don’t. If you still think you know better, be careful and have fun. And don’t mess it up (I mean it).
- If `is_valid_bit_pattern``bits`must also be valid for an instance of`Self`.
- Probably more, don’t mess it up (I mean it 2.0)

# tap/conv.rs

[1](https://fizyk20.github.io#1)/*! # Method-Directed Type Conversion
[2](https://fizyk20.github.io#2)
[3](https://fizyk20.github.io#3)The `std::convert` module provides traits for converting values from one type to
[4](https://fizyk20.github.io#4)another. The first of these, [`From<T>`], provides an associated function
[5](https://fizyk20.github.io#5)[`from(orig: T) -> Self`]. This function can only be called in prefix-position,
[6](https://fizyk20.github.io#6)as it does not have a `self` receiver. The second, [`Into<T>`], provides a
[7](https://fizyk20.github.io#7)method [`into(self) -> T`] which *can* be called in suffix-position; due to
[8](https://fizyk20.github.io#8)intractable problems in the type solver, this method cannot have any *further*
[9](https://fizyk20.github.io#9)method calls attached to it. It must be bound directly into a `let` or function
[10](https://fizyk20.github.io#10)call.
[11](https://fizyk20.github.io#11)
[12](https://fizyk20.github.io#12)The [`TryFrom<T>`] and [`TryInto<T>`] traits have the same properties, but
[13](https://fizyk20.github.io#13)permit failure.
[14](https://fizyk20.github.io#14)
[15](https://fizyk20.github.io#15)This module provides traits that place the conversion type parameter in the
[16](https://fizyk20.github.io#16)method, rather than in the trait, so that users can write `.conv::<T>()` to
[17](https://fizyk20.github.io#17)convert the preceding expression into `T`, without causing any failures in the
[18](https://fizyk20.github.io#18)type solver. These traits are blanket-implemented on all types that have an
[19](https://fizyk20.github.io#19)`Into<T>` implementation, which covers both the blanket implementation of `Into`
[20](https://fizyk20.github.io#20)for types with `From`, and manual implementations of `Into`.
[21](https://fizyk20.github.io#21)
[22](https://fizyk20.github.io#22)[`From<T>`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/convert/trait.From.html

# serde_core/de/mod.rs

[1](https://fizyk20.github.io#1)//! Generic data structure deserialization framework.
[2](https://fizyk20.github.io#2)//!
[3](https://fizyk20.github.io#3)//! The two most important traits in this module are [`Deserialize`] and
[4](https://fizyk20.github.io#4)//! [`Deserializer`].
[5](https://fizyk20.github.io#5)//!
[6](https://fizyk20.github.io#6)//!  - **A type that implements `Deserialize` is a data structure** that can be
[7](https://fizyk20.github.io#7)//!    deserialized from any data format supported by Serde, and conversely
[8](https://fizyk20.github.io#8)//!  - **A type that implements `Deserializer` is a data format** that can
[9](https://fizyk20.github.io#9)//!    deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
[10](https://fizyk20.github.io#10)//!
[11](https://fizyk20.github.io#11)//! # The Deserialize trait
[12](https://fizyk20.github.io#12)//!
[13](https://fizyk20.github.io#13)//! Serde provides [`Deserialize`] implementations for many Rust primitive and
[14](https://fizyk20.github.io#14)//! standard library types. The complete list is below. All of these can be
[15](https://fizyk20.github.io#15)//! deserialized using Serde out of the box.
[16](https://fizyk20.github.io#16)//!
[17](https://fizyk20.github.io#17)//! Additionally, Serde provides a procedural macro called [`serde_derive`] to
[18](https://fizyk20.github.io#18)//! automatically generate [`Deserialize`] implementations for structs and enums
[19](https://fizyk20.github.io#19)//! in your program. See the [derive section of the manual] for how to use this.
[20](https://fizyk20.github.io#20)//!
[21](https://fizyk20.github.io#21)//! In rare cases it may be necessary to implement [`Deserialize`] manually for
[22](https://fizyk20.github.io#22)//! some type in your program. See the [Implementing `Deserialize`] section of
[23](https://fizyk20.github.io#23)//! the manual for more about this.
[24](https://fizyk20.github.io#24)//!
[25](https://fizyk20.github.io#25)//! Third-party crates may provide [`Deserialize`] implementations for types
[26](https://fizyk20.github.io#26)//! that they expose. For example the [`linked-hash-map`] crate provides a
[27](https://fizyk20.github.io#27)//! [`LinkedHashMap<K, V>`] type that is deserializable by Serde because the
[28](https://fizyk20.github.io#28)//! crate provides an implementation of [`Deserialize`] for it.
[29](https://fizyk20.github.io#29)//!
[30](https://fizyk20.github.io#30)//! # The Deserializer trait
[31](https://fizyk20.github.io#31)//!
[32](https://fizyk20.github.io#32)//! [`Deserializer`] implementations are provided by third-party crates, for
[33](https://fizyk20.github.io#33)//! example [`serde_json`], [`serde_yaml`] and [`postcard`].
[34](https://fizyk20.github.io#34)//!
[35](https://fizyk20.github.io#35)//! A partial list of well-maintained formats is given on the [Serde
[36](https://fizyk20.github.io#36)//! website][data formats].
[37](https://fizyk20.github.io#37)//!
[38](https://fizyk20.github.io#38)//! # Implementations of Deserialize provided by Serde
[39](https://fizyk20.github.io#39)//!
[40](https://fizyk20.github.io#40)//! This is a slightly different set of types than what is supported for
[41](https://fizyk20.github.io#41)//! serialization. Some types can be serialized by Serde but not deserialized.
[42](https://fizyk20.github.io#42)//! One example is `OsStr`.
[43](https://fizyk20.github.io#43)//!
[44](https://fizyk20.github.io#44)//!  - **Primitive types**:
[45](https://fizyk20.github.io#45)//!    - bool
[46](https://fizyk20.github.io#46)//!    - i8, i16, i32, i64, i128, isize
[47](https://fizyk20.github.io#47)//!    - u8, u16, u32, u64, u128, usize
[48](https://fizyk20.github.io#48)//!    - f32, f64
