[1837](https://fizyk20.github.io#1837)pub trait MapAccess<'de> {
[1838](https://fizyk20.github.io#1838)    /// The error type that can be returned if some error occurs during
[1839](https://fizyk20.github.io#1839)    /// deserialization.
[1840](https://fizyk20.github.io#1840)    type Error: Error;
[1841](https://fizyk20.github.io#1841)
[1842](https://fizyk20.github.io#1842)    /// This returns `Ok(Some(key))` for the next key in the map, or `Ok(None)`
[1843](https://fizyk20.github.io#1843)    /// if there are no more remaining entries.
[1844](https://fizyk20.github.io#1844)    ///
[1845](https://fizyk20.github.io#1845)    /// `Deserialize` implementations should typically use
[1846](https://fizyk20.github.io#1846)    /// `MapAccess::next_key` or `MapAccess::next_entry` instead.
[1847](https://fizyk20.github.io#1847)    fn next_key_seed<K>(&mut self, seed: K) -> Result<Option<K::Value>, Self::Error>
[1848](https://fizyk20.github.io#1848)    where
[1849](https://fizyk20.github.io#1849)        K: DeserializeSeed<'de>;
[1850](https://fizyk20.github.io#1850)
[1851](https://fizyk20.github.io#1851)    /// This returns a `Ok(value)` for the next value in the map.
[1852](https://fizyk20.github.io#1852)    ///
[1853](https://fizyk20.github.io#1853)    /// `Deserialize` implementations should typically use
[1854](https://fizyk20.github.io#1854)    /// `MapAccess::next_value` instead.
[1855](https://fizyk20.github.io#1855)    ///
[1856](https://fizyk20.github.io#1856)    /// # Panics
[1857](https://fizyk20.github.io#1857)    ///
[1858](https://fizyk20.github.io#1858)    /// Calling `next_value_seed` before `next_key_seed` is incorrect and is
[1859](https://fizyk20.github.io#1859)    /// allowed to panic or return bogus results.
[1860](https://fizyk20.github.io#1860)    fn next_value_seed<V>(&mut self, seed: V) -> Result<V::Value, Self::Error>
[1861](https://fizyk20.github.io#1861)    where
[1862](https://fizyk20.github.io#1862)        V: DeserializeSeed<'de>;
[1863](https://fizyk20.github.io#1863)
[1864](https://fizyk20.github.io#1864)    /// This returns `Ok(Some((key, value)))` for the next (key-value) pair in
[1865](https://fizyk20.github.io#1865)    /// the map, or `Ok(None)` if there are no more remaining items.
[1866](https://fizyk20.github.io#1866)    ///
[1867](https://fizyk20.github.io#1867)    /// `MapAccess` implementations should override the default behavior if a
[1868](https://fizyk20.github.io#1868)    /// more efficient implementation is possible.
[1869](https://fizyk20.github.io#1869)    ///
[1870](https://fizyk20.github.io#1870)    /// `Deserialize` implementations should typically use
[1871](https://fizyk20.github.io#1871)    /// `MapAccess::next_entry` instead.
[1872](https://fizyk20.github.io#1872)    #[inline]
[1873](https://fizyk20.github.io#1873)    fn next_entry_seed<K, V>(
[1874](https://fizyk20.github.io#1874)        &mut self,
[1875](https://fizyk20.github.io#1875)        kseed: K,
[1876](https://fizyk20.github.io#1876)        vseed: V,
[1877](https://fizyk20.github.io#1877)    ) -> Result<Option<(K::Value, V::Value)>, Self::Error>
[1878](https://fizyk20.github.io#1878)    where
[1879](https://fizyk20.github.io#1879)        K: DeserializeSeed<'de>,
[1880](https://fizyk20.github.io#1880)        V: DeserializeSeed<'de>,
[1881](https://fizyk20.github.io#1881)    {
[1882](https://fizyk20.github.io#1882)        match tri!(self.next_key_seed(kseed)) {
[1883](https://fizyk20.github.io#1883)            Some(key) => {
[1884](https://fizyk20.github.io#1884)                let value = tri!(self.next_value_seed(vseed));
[1885](https://fizyk20.github.io#1885)                Ok(Some((key, value)))
[1886](https://fizyk20.github.io#1886)            }
[1887](https://fizyk20.github.io#1887)            None => Ok(None),
[1888](https://fizyk20.github.io#1888)        }
[1889](https://fizyk20.github.io#1889)    }
[1890](https://fizyk20.github.io#1890)
[1891](https://fizyk20.github.io#1891)    /// This returns `Ok(Some(key))` for the next key in the map, or `Ok(None)`
[1892](https://fizyk20.github.io#1892)    /// if there are no more remaining entries.
[1893](https://fizyk20.github.io#1893)    ///
[1894](https://fizyk20.github.io#1894)    /// This method exists as a convenience for `Deserialize` implementations.
[1895](https://fizyk20.github.io#1895)    /// `MapAccess` implementations should not override the default behavior.
[1896](https://fizyk20.github.io#1896)    #[inline]
[1897](https://fizyk20.github.io#1897)    fn next_key<K>(&mut self) -> Result<Option<K>, Self::Error>
[1898](https://fizyk20.github.io#1898)    where
[1899](https://fizyk20.github.io#1899)        K: Deserialize<'de>,
[1900](https://fizyk20.github.io#1900)    {
[1901](https://fizyk20.github.io#1901)        self.next_key_seed(PhantomData)
[1902](https://fizyk20.github.io#1902)    }

[1905](https://fizyk20.github.io#1905)    ///
[1906](https://fizyk20.github.io#1906)    /// This method exists as a convenience for `Deserialize` implementations.

[1908](https://fizyk20.github.io#1908)    ///

[1910](https://fizyk20.github.io#1910)    ///

[1917](https://fizyk20.github.io#1917)    {
[1918](https://fizyk20.github.io#1918)        self.next_value_seed(PhantomData)
[1919](https://fizyk20.github.io#1919)    }
[1920](https://fizyk20.github.io#1920)
[1921](https://fizyk20.github.io#1921)    /// This returns `Ok(Some((key, value)))` for the next (key-value) pair in

[2284](https://fizyk20.github.io#2284)/// Converts an existing value into a `Deserializer` from which other values can
[2285](https://fizyk20.github.io#2285)/// be deserialized.
[2286](https://fizyk20.github.io#2286)///
[2287](https://fizyk20.github.io#2287)/// # Lifetime
[2288](https://fizyk20.github.io#2288)///
[2289](https://fizyk20.github.io#2289)/// The `'de` lifetime of this trait is the lifetime of data that may be
[2290](https://fizyk20.github.io#2290)/// borrowed from the resulting `Deserializer`. See the page [Understanding
[2291](https://fizyk20.github.io#2291)/// deserializer lifetimes] for a more detailed explanation of these lifetimes.
[2292](https://fizyk20.github.io#2292)///
[2293](https://fizyk20.github.io#2293)/// [Understanding deserializer lifetimes]: https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html
[2294](https://fizyk20.github.io#2294)///
[2295](https://fizyk20.github.io#2295)/// # Example
[2296](https://fizyk20.github.io#2296)///
[2297](https://fizyk20.github.io#2297)/// ```edition2021
[2298](https://fizyk20.github.io#2298)/// use serde::de::{value, Deserialize, IntoDeserializer};
[2299](https://fizyk20.github.io#2299)/// use serde_derive::Deserialize;
[2300](https://fizyk20.github.io#2300)/// use std::str::FromStr;
[2301](https://fizyk20.github.io#2301)///
[2302](https://fizyk20.github.io#2302)/// #[derive(Deserialize)]
[2303](https://fizyk20.github.io#2303)/// enum Setting {
[2304](https://fizyk20.github.io#2304)///     On,
[2305](https://fizyk20.github.io#2305)///     Off,
[2306](https://fizyk20.github.io#2306)/// }
[2307](https://fizyk20.github.io#2307)///
[2308](https://fizyk20.github.io#2308)/// impl FromStr for Setting {
[2309](https://fizyk20.github.io#2309)///     type Err = value::Error;
[2310](https://fizyk20.github.io#2310)///
[2311](https://fizyk20.github.io#2311)///     fn from_str(s: &str) -> Result<Self, Self::Err> {
[2312](https://fizyk20.github.io#2312)///         Self::deserialize(s.into_deserializer())
[2313](https://fizyk20.github.io#2313)///     }
[2314](https://fizyk20.github.io#2314)/// }
[2315](https://fizyk20.github.io#2315)/// ```
[2316](https://fizyk20.github.io#2316)pub trait IntoDeserializer<'de, E: Error = value::Error> {
[2317](https://fizyk20.github.io#2317)    /// The type of the deserializer being converted into.
[2318](https://fizyk20.github.io#2318)    type Deserializer: Deserializer<'de, Error = E>;
[2319](https://fizyk20.github.io#2319)
[2320](https://fizyk20.github.io#2320)    /// Convert this value into a deserializer.
[2321](https://fizyk20.github.io#2321)    fn into_deserializer(self) -> Self::Deserializer;
[2322](https://fizyk20.github.io#2322)}

[2325](https://fizyk20.github.io#2325)
[2326](https://fizyk20.github.io#2326)/// Used in error messages.
[2327](https://fizyk20.github.io#2327)///
[2328](https://fizyk20.github.io#2328)/// - expected `a`
[2329](https://fizyk20.github.io#2329)/// - expected `a` or `b`
[2330](https://fizyk20.github.io#2330)/// - expected one of `a`, `b`, `c`
[2331](https://fizyk20.github.io#2331)///
[2332](https://fizyk20.github.io#2332)/// The slice of names must not be empty.
[2333](https://fizyk20.github.io#2333)struct OneOf {
[2334](https://fizyk20.github.io#2334)    names: &'static [&'static str],
[2335](https://fizyk20.github.io#2335)}
[2336](https://fizyk20.github.io#2336)
[2337](https://fizyk20.github.io#2337)impl Display for OneOf {
[2338](https://fizyk20.github.io#2338)    fn fmt(&self, formatter: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[2339](https://fizyk20.github.io#2339)        match self.names.len() {
[2340](https://fizyk20.github.io#2340)            0 => panic!(), // special case elsewhere
[2341](https://fizyk20.github.io#2341)            1 => write!(formatter, "`{}`", self.names[0]),
[2342](https://fizyk20.github.io#2342)            2 => write!(formatter, "`{}` or `{}`", self.names[0], self.names[1]),
[2343](https://fizyk20.github.io#2343)            _ => {
[2344](https://fizyk20.github.io#2344)                tri!(formatter.write_str("one of "));
[2345](https://fizyk20.github.io#2345)                for (i, alt) in self.names.iter().enumerate() {
[2346](https://fizyk20.github.io#2346)                    if i > 0 {
[2347](https://fizyk20.github.io#2347)                        tri!(formatter.write_str(", "));
[2348](https://fizyk20.github.io#2348)                    }
[2349](https://fizyk20.github.io#2349)                    tri!(write!(formatter, "`{}`", alt));
[2350](https://fizyk20.github.io#2350)                }
[2351](https://fizyk20.github.io#2351)                Ok(())
[2352](https://fizyk20.github.io#2352)            }
[2353](https://fizyk20.github.io#2353)        }
[2354](https://fizyk20.github.io#2354)    }
[2355](https://fizyk20.github.io#2355)}

# DeserializeOwned in serde_core::de - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/serde_core/de/trait.DeserializeOwned.html

`pub trait DeserializeOwned: for<'de> `[Deserialize](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Deserialize.html)<'de> { }## Expand description

A data structure that can be deserialized without borrowing any data from the deserializer.

This is primarily useful for trait bounds on functions. For example a
`from_str` function may be able to deserialize a data structure that borrows
from the input string, but a `from_reader` function may only deserialize
owned data.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
fn from_str<'a, T>(s: &'a str) -> Result<T>
where
    T: Deserialize<'a>;
fn from_reader<R, T>(rdr: R) -> Result<T>
where
    R: Read,
    T: DeserializeOwned;
```
[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#lifetime)Lifetime

The relationship between `Deserialize` and `DeserializeOwned` in trait
bounds is explained in more detail on the page [Understanding deserializer
lifetimes](https://serde.rs/lifetimes.html).

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

Causes `self` to use its `UpperHex` implementation when
`Debug`-formatted.

Formats each item in a sequence.

This wrapper structure conditionally implements all of the formatting
traits when `self` can be viewed as an iterator whose *items* implement
them. It iterates over `&self` and prints each item according to the
formatting specifier provided.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

[4](https://fizyk20.github.io#4)  NonZeroU128, NonZeroU16, NonZeroU32, NonZeroU64, NonZeroU8, NonZeroUsize,
[5](https://fizyk20.github.io#5)};
[6](https://fizyk20.github.io#6)
[7](https://fizyk20.github.io#7)/// Marker trait for "plain old data" types with no uninit (or padding) bytes.
[8](https://fizyk20.github.io#8)///
[9](https://fizyk20.github.io#9)/// The requirements for this is very similar to [`Pod`],
[10](https://fizyk20.github.io#10)/// except that it doesn't require that all bit patterns of the type are valid,
[11](https://fizyk20.github.io#11)/// i.e. it does not require the type to be [`Zeroable`][crate::Zeroable].
[12](https://fizyk20.github.io#12)/// This limits what you can do with a type of this kind, but also broadens the
[13](https://fizyk20.github.io#13)/// included types to things like C-style enums. Notably, you can only cast from
[14](https://fizyk20.github.io#14)/// *immutable* references to a [`NoUninit`] type into *immutable* references of
[15](https://fizyk20.github.io#15)/// any other type, no casting of mutable references or mutable references to
[16](https://fizyk20.github.io#16)/// slices etc.
[17](https://fizyk20.github.io#17)///
[18](https://fizyk20.github.io#18)/// [`Pod`] is a subset of [`NoUninit`], meaning that any `T: Pod` is also
[19](https://fizyk20.github.io#19)/// [`NoUninit`] but any `T: NoUninit` is not necessarily [`Pod`]. If possible,
[20](https://fizyk20.github.io#20)/// prefer implementing [`Pod`] directly. To get more [`Pod`]-like functionality
[21](https://fizyk20.github.io#21)/// for a type that is only [`NoUninit`], consider also implementing
[22](https://fizyk20.github.io#22)/// [`CheckedBitPattern`][crate::CheckedBitPattern].
[23](https://fizyk20.github.io#23)///
[24](https://fizyk20.github.io#24)/// The rules for padding for various types and representations are documented
[25](https://fizyk20.github.io#25)/// in the Rust reference section on [type layout].
[26](https://fizyk20.github.io#26)///
[27](https://fizyk20.github.io#27)/// # Derive
[28](https://fizyk20.github.io#28)///
[29](https://fizyk20.github.io#29)/// A `#[derive(NoUninit)]` macro is provided under the `derive` feature flag
[30](https://fizyk20.github.io#30)/// which will automatically validate the requirements of this trait and
[31](https://fizyk20.github.io#31)/// implement the trait for you for both enums and structs. This is the
[32](https://fizyk20.github.io#32)/// recommended method for implementing the trait, however it's also possible to
[33](https://fizyk20.github.io#33)/// do manually. If you implement it manually, you *must* carefully follow the
[34](https://fizyk20.github.io#34)/// below safety rules.
[35](https://fizyk20.github.io#35)///
[36](https://fizyk20.github.io#36)/// # Safety
[37](https://fizyk20.github.io#37)///
[38](https://fizyk20.github.io#38)/// The same as [`Pod`] except we disregard the rule about it must
[39](https://fizyk20.github.io#39)/// allow any bit pattern (i.e. it does not need to be
[40](https://fizyk20.github.io#40)/// [`Zeroable`][crate::Zeroable]). Still, this is a quite strong guarantee
[41](https://fizyk20.github.io#41)/// about a type, so *be careful* whem implementing it manually.
[42](https://fizyk20.github.io#42)///
[43](https://fizyk20.github.io#43)/// * The type must be inhabited (eg: no
[44](https://fizyk20.github.io#44)///   [Infallible](core::convert::Infallible)).
[45](https://fizyk20.github.io#45)/// * The type must not contain any uninit (or padding) bytes, either in the
[46](https://fizyk20.github.io#46)///   middle or on the end (eg: no `#[repr(C)] struct Foo(u8, u16)`, which has
[47](https://fizyk20.github.io#47)///   padding in the middle, and also no `#[repr(C)] struct Foo(u16, u8)`, which
[48](https://fizyk20.github.io#48)///   has padding on the end).
[49](https://fizyk20.github.io#49)/// * Structs need to have all fields also be `NoUninit`.
[50](https://fizyk20.github.io#50)/// * Structs need to be `repr(C)` or `repr(transparent)`. In the case of
[51](https://fizyk20.github.io#51)///   `repr(C)`, the `packed` and `align` repr modifiers can be used as long as
[52](https://fizyk20.github.io#52)///   all other rules end up being followed.
[53](https://fizyk20.github.io#53)/// * Enums need to be `#[repr(Int)]`, `#[repr(C)]`, or both.
[54](https://fizyk20.github.io#54)/// * Enums may have fields. If the enum has fields,
[55](https://fizyk20.github.io#55)///     * Each variant's fields must individually follow the same rules as a struct
[56](https://fizyk20.github.io#56)///     * All variants must be the same size, and require no padding-to-alignment
[57](https://fizyk20.github.io#57)///     * There must be no padding needed between the discriminant type and the
[58](https://fizyk20.github.io#58)///       "fields struct" of any variant
[59](https://fizyk20.github.io#59)/// * It is disallowed for types to contain pointer types, `Cell`, `UnsafeCell`,
[60](https://fizyk20.github.io#60)///   atomics, and any other forms of interior mutability.
[61](https://fizyk20.github.io#61)/// * More precisely: A shared reference to the type must allow reads, and
[62](https://fizyk20.github.io#62)///   *only* reads. RustBelt's separation logic is based on the notion that a
[63](https://fizyk20.github.io#63)///   type is allowed to define a sharing predicate, its own invariant that must
[64](https://fizyk20.github.io#64)///   hold for shared references, and this predicate is the reasoning that allow
[65](https://fizyk20.github.io#65)///   it to deal with atomic and cells etc. We require the sharing predicate to
[66](https://fizyk20.github.io#66)///   be trivial and permit only read-only access.
[67](https://fizyk20.github.io#67)/// * There's probably more, don't mess it up (I mean it).
[68](https://fizyk20.github.io#68)///
[69](https://fizyk20.github.io#69)/// [type layout]: <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/type-layout.html>
[70](https://fizyk20.github.io#70)pub unsafe trait NoUninit: Sized + Copy + 'static {}
[71](https://fizyk20.github.io#71)
[72](https://fizyk20.github.io#72)unsafe impl<T: Pod> NoUninit for T {}
[73](https://fizyk20.github.io#73)

[75](https://fizyk20.github.io#75)
[76](https://fizyk20.github.io#76)unsafe impl NoUninit for bool {}

[78](https://fizyk20.github.io#78)unsafe impl NoUninit for NonZeroU8 {}
[79](https://fizyk20.github.io#79)unsafe impl NoUninit for NonZeroI8 {}

[81](https://fizyk20.github.io#81)unsafe impl NoUninit for NonZeroI16 {}

# pipe.rs - source

# tap/pipe.rs

[1](https://fizyk20.github.io#1)/*! # Universal Suffix Calls
[2](https://fizyk20.github.io#2)
[3](https://fizyk20.github.io#3)This module provides a single trait, `Pipe`, which provides a number of methods
[4](https://fizyk20.github.io#4)useful for placing functions in suffix position. The most common method, `pipe`,
[5](https://fizyk20.github.io#5)forwards a value `T` into any function `T -> R`, returning `R`. The other
[6](https://fizyk20.github.io#6)methods all apply some form of borrowing to the value before passing the borrow
[7](https://fizyk20.github.io#7)into the piped function. These are of less value, but provided to maintain a
[8](https://fizyk20.github.io#8)similar API to the `tap` module’s methods, and for convenience in the event that
[9](https://fizyk20.github.io#9)you do have a use for them.
[10](https://fizyk20.github.io#10)
[11](https://fizyk20.github.io#11)This module is as much of a [UFCS] method syntax that can be provided as a
[12](https://fizyk20.github.io#12)library, rather than in the language grammar.
[13](https://fizyk20.github.io#13)
[14](https://fizyk20.github.io#14)[UFCS]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Function_Call_Syntax
[15](https://fizyk20.github.io#15)!*/
[16](https://fizyk20.github.io#16)
[17](https://fizyk20.github.io#17)use core::{
[18](https://fizyk20.github.io#18)	borrow::{Borrow, BorrowMut},
[19](https://fizyk20.github.io#19)	ops::{Deref, DerefMut},
[20](https://fizyk20.github.io#20)};
[21](https://fizyk20.github.io#21)
[22](https://fizyk20.github.io#22)/** Provides universal suffix-position call syntax for any function.
[23](https://fizyk20.github.io#23)
[24](https://fizyk20.github.io#24)This trait provides methods that allow any closure or free function to be placed
[25](https://fizyk20.github.io#25)as a suffix-position call, by writing them as
[26](https://fizyk20.github.io#26)
[27](https://fizyk20.github.io#27)```rust
[28](https://fizyk20.github.io#28)# use tap::pipe::Pipe;
[29](https://fizyk20.github.io#29)# let receiver = 5;
[30](https://fizyk20.github.io#30)fn not_a_method(x: i32) -> u8 { x as u8 }
[31](https://fizyk20.github.io#31)receiver.pipe(not_a_method);
[32](https://fizyk20.github.io#32)```
[33](https://fizyk20.github.io#33)
[34](https://fizyk20.github.io#34)Piping into functions that take more than one argument still requires writing a
[35](https://fizyk20.github.io#35)closure with ordinary function-call syntax. This is after all only a library,
[36](https://fizyk20.github.io#36)not a syntax transformation:
[37](https://fizyk20.github.io#37)
[38](https://fizyk20.github.io#38)```rust
[39](https://fizyk20.github.io#39)use tap::pipe::Pipe;
[40](https://fizyk20.github.io#40)fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32 { x + y }
[41](https://fizyk20.github.io#41)
[42](https://fizyk20.github.io#42)let out = 5.pipe(|x| add(x, 10));
[43](https://fizyk20.github.io#43)assert_eq!(out, 15);
[44](https://fizyk20.github.io#44)```
[45](https://fizyk20.github.io#45)
[46](https://fizyk20.github.io#46)Like tapping, piping is useful for cases where you want to write a sequence of
[47](https://fizyk20.github.io#47)processing steps without introducing many intermediate bindings, and your steps
[48](https://fizyk20.github.io#48)contain functions which are not eligible for dot-call syntax.
[49](https://fizyk20.github.io#49)
[50](https://fizyk20.github.io#50)The main difference between piping and tapping is that tapping always returns
[51](https://fizyk20.github.io#51)the value that was passed into the tap, while piping forwards the value into the
[52](https://fizyk20.github.io#52)effect function, and returns the output of evaluating the effect function with
[53](https://fizyk20.github.io#53)the value. Piping is a transformation, not merely an inspection or modification.
[54](https://fizyk20.github.io#54)**/
[55](https://fizyk20.github.io#55)pub trait Pipe {
[56](https://fizyk20.github.io#56)	/// Pipes by value. This is generally the method you want to use.
[57](https://fizyk20.github.io#57)	///
[58](https://fizyk20.github.io#58)	/// # Examples
[59](https://fizyk20.github.io#59)	///
[60](https://fizyk20.github.io#60)	/// ```rust
[61](https://fizyk20.github.io#61)	/// use tap::pipe::Pipe;
[62](https://fizyk20.github.io#62)	///
[63](https://fizyk20.github.io#63)	/// fn triple(x: i32) -> i64 {
[64](https://fizyk20.github.io#64)	///   x as i64 * 3
[65](https://fizyk20.github.io#65)	/// }
[66](https://fizyk20.github.io#66)	///
[67](https://fizyk20.github.io#67)	/// assert_eq!(
[68](https://fizyk20.github.io#68)	///   10.pipe(triple),
[69](https://fizyk20.github.io#69)	///   30,
[70](https://fizyk20.github.io#70)	/// );
[71](https://fizyk20.github.io#71)	/// ```
[72](https://fizyk20.github.io#72)	#[inline(always)]
[73](https://fizyk20.github.io#73)	fn pipe<R>(self, func: impl FnOnce(Self) -> R) -> R
[74](https://fizyk20.github.io#74)	where
[75](https://fizyk20.github.io#75)		Self: Sized,
[76](https://fizyk20.github.io#76)		R: Sized,

[78](https://fizyk20.github.io#78)		func(self)
[79](https://fizyk20.github.io#79)	}

[81](https://fizyk20.github.io#81)	/// Borrows `self` and passes that borrow into the pipe function.

[83](https://fizyk20.github.io#83)	/// # Examples
[84](https://fizyk20.github.io#84)	///

[91](https://fizyk20.github.io#91)	/// let vec = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];

[104](https://fizyk20.github.io#104)	/// Mutably borrows `self` and passes that borrow into the pipe function.

[107](https://fizyk20.github.io#107)	///

[112](https://fizyk20.github.io#112)	/// let last = vec

}## Expand description

Provides universal suffix-position call syntax for any function.

This trait provides methods that allow any closure or free function to be placed as a suffix-position call, by writing them as

```
fn not_a_method(x: i32) -> u8 { x as u8 }
receiver.pipe(not_a_method);
```
Piping into functions that take more than one argument still requires writing a closure with ordinary function-call syntax. This is after all only a library, not a syntax transformation:

```
use tap::pipe::Pipe;
fn add(x: i32, y: i32) -> i32 { x + y }
let out = 5.pipe(|x| add(x, 10));
assert_eq!(out, 15);
```
Like tapping, piping is useful for cases where you want to write a sequence of processing steps without introducing many intermediate bindings, and your steps contain functions which are not eligible for dot-call syntax.

The main difference between piping and tapping is that tapping always returns the value that was passed into the tap, while piping forwards the value into the effect function, and returns the output of evaluating the effect function with the value. Piping is a transformation, not merely an inspection or modification.

## Provided Methods[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#provided-methods)

Borrows `self` and passes that borrow into the pipe function.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#examples-1)Examples

```
use tap::pipe::Pipe;
fn fold(v: &Vec<i32>) -> i32 {
  v.iter().copied().sum()
}
let vec = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let sum = vec.pipe_ref(fold);
assert_eq!(sum, 15);
assert_eq!(vec.len(), 5);
```

[102](https://fizyk20.github.io#102)        impl<U: Unsigned, B: Bit> Pow<UInt<U, B>> for $t {
[103](https://fizyk20.github.io#103)            type Output = $t;
[104](https://fizyk20.github.io#104)            // powi is unstable in core, so we have to write this function ourselves.
[105](https://fizyk20.github.io#105)            // copied from num::pow::pow
[106](https://fizyk20.github.io#106)            #[inline]
[107](https://fizyk20.github.io#107)            fn powi(self, _: UInt<U, B>) -> Self::Output {
[108](https://fizyk20.github.io#108)                let mut exp = <UInt<U, B> as Unsigned>::to_u32();
[109](https://fizyk20.github.io#109)                let mut base = self;
[110](https://fizyk20.github.io#110)
[111](https://fizyk20.github.io#111)                if exp == 0 {
[112](https://fizyk20.github.io#112)                    return 1.0;
[113](https://fizyk20.github.io#113)                }
[114](https://fizyk20.github.io#114)
[115](https://fizyk20.github.io#115)                while exp & 1 == 0 {
[116](https://fizyk20.github.io#116)                    base *= base;
[117](https://fizyk20.github.io#117)                    exp >>= 1;
[118](https://fizyk20.github.io#118)                }
[119](https://fizyk20.github.io#119)                if exp == 1 {
[120](https://fizyk20.github.io#120)                    return base;
[121](https://fizyk20.github.io#121)                }
[122](https://fizyk20.github.io#122)
[123](https://fizyk20.github.io#123)                let mut acc = base.clone();
[124](https://fizyk20.github.io#124)                while exp > 1 {
[125](https://fizyk20.github.io#125)                    exp >>= 1;
[126](https://fizyk20.github.io#126)                    base *= base;
[127](https://fizyk20.github.io#127)                    if exp & 1 == 1 {
[128](https://fizyk20.github.io#128)                        acc *= base.clone();
[129](https://fizyk20.github.io#129)                    }
[130](https://fizyk20.github.io#130)                }
[131](https://fizyk20.github.io#131)                acc
[132](https://fizyk20.github.io#132)            }
[133](https://fizyk20.github.io#133)        }
[134](https://fizyk20.github.io#134)
[135](https://fizyk20.github.io#135)        impl Pow<Z0> for $t {
[136](https://fizyk20.github.io#136)            type Output = $t;
[137](https://fizyk20.github.io#137)            #[inline]
[138](https://fizyk20.github.io#138)            fn powi(self, _: Z0) -> Self::Output {
[139](https://fizyk20.github.io#139)                1.0
[140](https://fizyk20.github.io#140)            }
[141](https://fizyk20.github.io#141)        }
[142](https://fizyk20.github.io#142)
[143](https://fizyk20.github.io#143)        impl<U: Unsigned + NonZero> Pow<PInt<U>> for $t {
[144](https://fizyk20.github.io#144)            type Output = $t;
[145](https://fizyk20.github.io#145)            // powi is unstable in core, so we have to write this function ourselves.
[146](https://fizyk20.github.io#146)            // copied from num::pow::pow
[147](https://fizyk20.github.io#147)            #[inline]
[148](https://fizyk20.github.io#148)            fn powi(self, _: PInt<U>) -> Self::Output {
[149](https://fizyk20.github.io#149)                let mut exp = U::to_u32();
[150](https://fizyk20.github.io#150)                let mut base = self;
[151](https://fizyk20.github.io#151)
[152](https://fizyk20.github.io#152)                if exp == 0 {
[153](https://fizyk20.github.io#153)                    return 1.0;
[154](https://fizyk20.github.io#154)                }
[155](https://fizyk20.github.io#155)
[156](https://fizyk20.github.io#156)                while exp & 1 == 0 {
[157](https://fizyk20.github.io#157)                    base *= base;
[158](https://fizyk20.github.io#158)                    exp >>= 1;
[159](https://fizyk20.github.io#159)                }
[160](https://fizyk20.github.io#160)                if exp == 1 {
[161](https://fizyk20.github.io#161)                    return base;
[162](https://fizyk20.github.io#162)                }
[163](https://fizyk20.github.io#163)
[164](https://fizyk20.github.io#164)                let mut acc = base.clone();
[165](https://fizyk20.github.io#165)                while exp > 1 {
[166](https://fizyk20.github.io#166)                    exp >>= 1;
[167](https://fizyk20.github.io#167)                    base *= base;
[168](https://fizyk20.github.io#168)                    if exp & 1 == 1 {
[169](https://fizyk20.github.io#169)                        acc *= base.clone();
[170](https://fizyk20.github.io#170)                    }
[171](https://fizyk20.github.io#171)                }
[172](https://fizyk20.github.io#172)                acc
[173](https://fizyk20.github.io#173)            }
[174](https://fizyk20.github.io#174)        }
[175](https://fizyk20.github.io#175)
[176](https://fizyk20.github.io#176)        impl<U: Unsigned + NonZero> Pow<NInt<U>> for $t {
[177](https://fizyk20.github.io#177)            type Output = $t;
[178](https://fizyk20.github.io#178)
[179](https://fizyk20.github.io#179)            #[inline]
[180](https://fizyk20.github.io#180)            fn powi(self, _: NInt<U>) -> Self::Output {
[181](https://fizyk20.github.io#181)                <$t as Pow<PInt<U>>>::powi(self, PInt::new()).recip()
[182](https://fizyk20.github.io#182)            }
[183](https://fizyk20.github.io#183)        }
[184](https://fizyk20.github.io#184)    };

[513](https://fizyk20.github.io#513)
[514](https://fizyk20.github.io#514)Due to the intricacies of the macro system, if the left-hand operand is more complex than a simple

[516](https://fizyk20.github.io#516)

[518](https://fizyk20.github.io#518)`cmp!(typenum::P5 > typenum::P3)`.
[519](https://fizyk20.github.io#519)
[520](https://fizyk20.github.io#520)The result of this comparison will always be one of `True` (aka `B1`) or `False` (aka `B0`).

# Same in typenum::type_operators - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/type_operators/trait.Same.html

```
pub trait Same<Rhs = Self> {
    type
```
[Output](https://fizyk20.github.io#associatedtype.Output);
}## Expand description

A **type operator** that ensures that `Rhs` is the same as `Self`, it is mainly useful
for writing macros that can take arbitrary binary or unary operators.

`Same` is implemented generically for all types; it should never need to be implemented
for anything else.

Note that Rust lazily evaluates types, so this will only fail for two different types if
the `Output` is used.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#example)Example

```
use typenum::{Same, Unsigned, U4, U5};
assert_eq!(<U5 as Same<U5>>::Output::to_u32(), 5);
// Only an error if we use it:
type Undefined = <U5 as Same<U4>>::Output;
// Compiler error:
// Undefined::to_u32();
```
## Required Associated Types[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#required-associated-types)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# tap.rs - source

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/src/tap/tap.rs.html

# tap/tap.rs

[1](https://fizyk20.github.io#1)/*! # Point-Free Inspection
[2](https://fizyk20.github.io#2)
[3](https://fizyk20.github.io#3)The standard library does not provide a way to view or modify an expression
[4](https://fizyk20.github.io#4)without binding it to a name. This module provides extension methods that take
[5](https://fizyk20.github.io#5)and return a value, allowing it to be temporarily bound without creating a new
[6](https://fizyk20.github.io#6)`let`-statement in the enclosing scope.
[7](https://fizyk20.github.io#7)
[8](https://fizyk20.github.io#8)The two main uses of these methods are to temporarily attach debugging
[9](https://fizyk20.github.io#9)tracepoints to an expression without modifying its surrounding code, or to
[10](https://fizyk20.github.io#10)temporarily mutate an otherwise-immutable object.
[11](https://fizyk20.github.io#11)
[12](https://fizyk20.github.io#12)For convenience, methods are available that will modify the *view* of the tapped
[13](https://fizyk20.github.io#13)object that is passed to the effect function, by using the value’s
[14](https://fizyk20.github.io#14)`Borrow`/`BorrowMut`, `AsRef`/`AsMut`, or `Index`/`IndexMut` trait
[15](https://fizyk20.github.io#15)implementations. For example, the `Vec` collection has no `fn sort` method: this
[16](https://fizyk20.github.io#16)is actually implemented on slices, to which `Vec` dereferences.
[17](https://fizyk20.github.io#17)
[18](https://fizyk20.github.io#18)```rust
[19](https://fizyk20.github.io#19)use tap::tap::*;
[20](https://fizyk20.github.io#20)# fn make_vec() -> Vec<i32> { vec![] }
[21](https://fizyk20.github.io#21)
[22](https://fizyk20.github.io#22)// taps take ordinary closures, which can use deref coercion
[23](https://fizyk20.github.io#23)make_vec().tap_mut(|v| v.sort());
[24](https://fizyk20.github.io#24)// `Vec<T>` implements `BorrowMut<[T]>`,
[25](https://fizyk20.github.io#25)make_vec().tap_borrow_mut(<[_]>::sort);
[26](https://fizyk20.github.io#26)// and `AsMut<[T]>`,
[27](https://fizyk20.github.io#27)make_vec().tap_ref_mut(<[_]>::sort);
[28](https://fizyk20.github.io#28)// and `DerefMut<Target = [T]>,
[29](https://fizyk20.github.io#29)make_vec().tap_deref_mut(<[_]>::sort);
[30](https://fizyk20.github.io#30)// but has no inherent method `sort`.
[31](https://fizyk20.github.io#31)// make_vec().tap_mut(Vec::sort);
[32](https://fizyk20.github.io#32)```
[33](https://fizyk20.github.io#33)!*/
[34](https://fizyk20.github.io#34)
[35](https://fizyk20.github.io#35)use core::{
[36](https://fizyk20.github.io#36)	borrow::{Borrow, BorrowMut},
[37](https://fizyk20.github.io#37)	ops::{Deref, DerefMut},
[38](https://fizyk20.github.io#38)};
[39](https://fizyk20.github.io#39)
[40](https://fizyk20.github.io#40)/** Point-free value inspection and modification.
[41](https://fizyk20.github.io#41)
[42](https://fizyk20.github.io#42)This trait provides methods that permit viewing the value of an expression
[43](https://fizyk20.github.io#43)without requiring a new `let` binding or any other alterations to the original
[44](https://fizyk20.github.io#44)code other than insertion of the `.tap()` call.
[45](https://fizyk20.github.io#45)
[46](https://fizyk20.github.io#46)The methods in this trait do not perform any view conversions on the value they
[47](https://fizyk20.github.io#47)receive; it is borrowed and passed directly to the effect argument.
[48](https://fizyk20.github.io#48)**/
[49](https://fizyk20.github.io#49)pub trait Tap
[50](https://fizyk20.github.io#50)where
[51](https://fizyk20.github.io#51)	Self: Sized,
[52](https://fizyk20.github.io#52){
[53](https://fizyk20.github.io#53)	/// Immutable access to a value.
[54](https://fizyk20.github.io#54)	///
[55](https://fizyk20.github.io#55)	/// This function permits a value to be viewed by some inspecting function
[56](https://fizyk20.github.io#56)	/// without affecting the overall shape of the expression that contains this
[57](https://fizyk20.github.io#57)	/// method call. It is useful for attaching assertions or logging points
[58](https://fizyk20.github.io#58)	/// into a multi-part expression.
[59](https://fizyk20.github.io#59)	///
[60](https://fizyk20.github.io#60)	/// # Examples
[61](https://fizyk20.github.io#61)	///
[62](https://fizyk20.github.io#62)	/// Here we use `.tap()` to attach logging tracepoints to each stage of a
[63](https://fizyk20.github.io#63)	/// value-processing pipeline.
[64](https://fizyk20.github.io#64)	///
[65](https://fizyk20.github.io#65)	/// ```rust
[66](https://fizyk20.github.io#66)	/// use tap::tap::Tap;
[67](https://fizyk20.github.io#67)	/// # struct Tmp;
[68](https://fizyk20.github.io#68)	/// # impl Tmp { fn process_value(self) -> Self { self } }
[69](https://fizyk20.github.io#69)	/// # fn make_value() -> Tmp { Tmp }
[70](https://fizyk20.github.io#70)	/// # macro_rules! log { ($msg:literal, $x:ident) => {{}}; }
[71](https://fizyk20.github.io#71)	///
[72](https://fizyk20.github.io#72)	/// let end = make_value()
[73](https://fizyk20.github.io#73)	///   // this line has no effect on the rest of the code
[74](https://fizyk20.github.io#74)	///   .tap(|v| log!("The produced value was: {}", v))
[75](https://fizyk20.github.io#75)	///   .process_value();
[76](https://fizyk20.github.io#76)	/// ```
[77](https://fizyk20.github.io#77)	#[inline(always)]
[78](https://fizyk20.github.io#78)	fn tap(self, func: impl FnOnce(&Self)) -> Self {
[79](https://fizyk20.github.io#79)		func(&self);
[80](https://fizyk20.github.io#80)		self
[81](https://fizyk20.github.io#81)	}
[82](https://fizyk20.github.io#82)
[83](https://fizyk20.github.io#83)	/// Mutable access to a value.
[84](https://fizyk20.github.io#84)	///
[85](https://fizyk20.github.io#85)	/// This function permits a value to be modified by some function without
[86](https://fizyk20.github.io#86)	/// affecting the overall shape of the expression that contains this method
[87](https://fizyk20.github.io#87)	/// call. It is useful for attaching modifier functions that have an
[88](https://fizyk20.github.io#88)	/// `&mut Self -> ()` signature to an expression, without requiring an
[89](https://fizyk20.github.io#89)	/// explicit `let mut` binding.
[90](https://fizyk20.github.io#90)	///
[91](https://fizyk20.github.io#91)	/// # Examples
[92](https://fizyk20.github.io#92)	///
[93](https://fizyk20.github.io#93)	/// Here we use `.tap_mut()` to sort an array without requring multiple
[94](https://fizyk20.github.io#94)	/// bindings.
[95](https://fizyk20.github.io#95)	///
[96](https://fizyk20.github.io#96)	/// ```rust
[97](https://fizyk20.github.io#97)	/// use tap::tap::Tap;
[98](https://fizyk20.github.io#98)	///
[99](https://fizyk20.github.io#99)	/// let sorted = [1i32, 5, 2, 4, 3]
[100](https://fizyk20.github.io#100)	///   .tap_mut(|arr| arr.sort());
[101](https://fizyk20.github.io#101)	/// assert_eq!(sorted, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
[102](https://fizyk20.github.io#102)	/// ```
[103](https://fizyk20.github.io#103)	///
[104](https://fizyk20.github.io#104)	/// Without tapping, this would be written as
[105](https://fizyk20.github.io#105)	///
[106](https://fizyk20.github.io#106)	/// ```rust
[107](https://fizyk20.github.io#107)	/// let mut received = [1, 5, 2, 4, 3];
[108](https://fizyk20.github.io#108)	/// received.sort();
[109](https://fizyk20.github.io#109)	/// let sorted = received;
[110](https://fizyk20.github.io#110)	/// ```
[111](https://fizyk20.github.io#111)	///
[112](https://fizyk20.github.io#112)	/// The mutable tap is a convenient alternative when the expression to
[113](https://fizyk20.github.io#113)	/// produce the collection is more complex, for example, an iterator
[114](https://fizyk20.github.io#114)	/// pipeline collected into a vector.
[115](https://fizyk20.github.io#115)	#[inline(always)]
[116](https://fizyk20.github.io#116)	fn tap_mut(mut self, func: impl FnOnce(&mut Self)) -> Self {
[117](https://fizyk20.github.io#117)		func(&mut self);
[118](https://fizyk20.github.io#118)		self
[119](https://fizyk20.github.io#119)	}
[120](https://fizyk20.github.io#120)
[121](https://fizyk20.github.io#121)	/// Immutable access to the `Borrow<B>` of a value.

[329](https://fizyk20.github.io#329)impl<T> Tap for T where T: Sized {}
[330](https://fizyk20.github.io#330)
[331](https://fizyk20.github.io#331)/** Optional tapping, conditional on the optional presence of a value.
[332](https://fizyk20.github.io#332)
[333](https://fizyk20.github.io#333)This trait is intended for use on types that express the concept of “optional
[334](https://fizyk20.github.io#334)presence”, primarily the [`Option`] monad. It provides taps that inspect the
[335](https://fizyk20.github.io#335)container to determine if the effect function should execute or not.
[336](https://fizyk20.github.io#336)
[337](https://fizyk20.github.io#337)> Note: This trait is a specialization of [`TapFallible`], and exists because
[338](https://fizyk20.github.io#338)> the [`std::ops::Try`] trait is still unstable. When `Try` stabilizes, this
[339](https://fizyk20.github.io#339)> trait can be removed, and `TapFallible` blanket-applied to all `Try`
[340](https://fizyk20.github.io#340)> implementors.
[341](https://fizyk20.github.io#341)
[342](https://fizyk20.github.io#342)[`Option`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/option/enum.Option.html
[343](https://fizyk20.github.io#343)[`TapFallible`]: trait.TapFallible.html
[344](https://fizyk20.github.io#344)[`std::ops::Try`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Try.html
[345](https://fizyk20.github.io#345)**/
[346](https://fizyk20.github.io#346)pub trait TapOptional
[347](https://fizyk20.github.io#347)where
[348](https://fizyk20.github.io#348)	Self: Sized,
[349](https://fizyk20.github.io#349){
[350](https://fizyk20.github.io#350)	/// The interior type that the container may or may not carry.
[351](https://fizyk20.github.io#351)	type Val: ?Sized;
[352](https://fizyk20.github.io#352)
[353](https://fizyk20.github.io#353)	/// Immutabily accesses an interior value only when it is present.
[354](https://fizyk20.github.io#354)	///
[355](https://fizyk20.github.io#355)	/// This function is identical to [`Tap::tap`], except that it is required
[356](https://fizyk20.github.io#356)	/// to check the implementing container for value presence before running.
[357](https://fizyk20.github.io#357)	/// Implementors must not run the effect function if the container is marked
[358](https://fizyk20.github.io#358)	/// as being empty.
[359](https://fizyk20.github.io#359)	///
[360](https://fizyk20.github.io#360)	/// [`Tap::tap`]: trait.Tap.html#method.tap
[361](https://fizyk20.github.io#361)	fn tap_some(self, func: impl FnOnce(&Self::Val)) -> Self;
[362](https://fizyk20.github.io#362)
[363](https://fizyk20.github.io#363)	/// Mutably accesses an interor value only when it is present.
[364](https://fizyk20.github.io#364)	///
[365](https://fizyk20.github.io#365)	/// This function is identical to [`Tap::tap_mut`], except that it is
[366](https://fizyk20.github.io#366)	/// required to check the implementing container for value presence before
[367](https://fizyk20.github.io#367)	/// running. Implementors must not run the effect function if the container
[368](https://fizyk20.github.io#368)	/// is marked as being empty.

[452](https://fizyk20.github.io#452)> [`std::ops::Try`] implementors. When `Try` stabilizes, this crate can be
[453](https://fizyk20.github.io#453)> updated to do so.

[tap_deref_mut_dbg](https://fizyk20.github.io#method.tap_deref_mut_dbg)<T>(self, func: impl [FnOnce](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnOnce.html)([&mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html))) -> Self
       where Self: [DerefMut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.DerefMut.html) + [Deref](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/deref/trait.Deref.html)<Target = T>,
             T: ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

Point-free value inspection and modification.

This trait provides methods that permit viewing the value of an expression
without requiring a new `let` binding or any other alterations to the original
code other than insertion of the `.tap()` call.

The methods in this trait do not perform any view conversions on the value they receive; it is borrowed and passed directly to the effect argument.

## Provided Methods[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#provided-methods)

Immutable access to a value.

This function permits a value to be viewed by some inspecting function without affecting the overall shape of the expression that contains this method call. It is useful for attaching assertions or logging points into a multi-part expression.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#examples)Examples

Here we use `.tap()` to attach logging tracepoints to each stage of a
value-processing pipeline.

```
use tap::tap::Tap;
let end = make_value()
  // this line has no effect on the rest of the code
  .tap(|v| log!("The produced value was: {}", v))
  .process_value();
```
Mutable access to a value.

This function permits a value to be modified by some function without
affecting the overall shape of the expression that contains this method
call. It is useful for attaching modifier functions that have an
`&mut Self -> ()` signature to an expression, without requiring an
explicit `let mut` binding.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#examples-1)Examples

Here we use `.tap_mut()` to sort an array without requring multiple
bindings.

```
use tap::tap::Tap;
let sorted = [1i32, 5, 2, 4, 3]
  .tap_mut(|arr| arr.sort());
assert_eq!(sorted, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]);
```
Without tapping, this would be written as

```
let mut received = [1, 5, 2, 4, 3];
received.sort();
let sorted = received;
```
The mutable tap is a convenient alternative when the expression to produce the collection is more complex, for example, an iterator pipeline collected into a vector.

# typenum::marker_traits - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/marker_traits/index.html

## Expand description

All of the **marker traits** used in typenum.

Note that the definition here for marker traits is slightly different than the conventional one – we include traits with functions that convert a type to the corresponding value, as well as associated constants that do the same.

For example, the `Integer` trait includes the function (among others) `fn to_i32() -> i32` and the associated constant `I32` so that one can do this:

```
use typenum::{Integer, N42};
assert_eq!(-42, N42::to_i32());
assert_eq!(-42, N42::I32);
```
## Traits[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#traits)

- [Bit](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Bit.html)
- The **marker trait**for compile time bits.
- [Integer](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Integer.html)
- The **marker trait**for compile time signed integers.
- [NonZero](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.NonZero.html)
- A **marker trait**to designate that a type is not zero. All number types in this crate implement`NonZero`except`B0`,`U0`, and`Z0`.
- [Ord](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Ord.html)
- A **Marker trait**for the types`Greater`,`Equal`, and`Less`.
- [Power](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.PowerOfTwo.html)- OfTwo
- The **marker trait**for type-level numbers which are a power of two.
- [Type](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.TypeArray.html)- Array
- The **marker trait**for type-level arrays of type-level numbers.
- [Unsigned](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Unsigned.html)
- The **marker trait**for compile time unsigned integers.
- [Zero](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Zero.html)
- A **marker trait**to designate that a type is zero. Only`B0`,`U0`, and`Z0`implement this trait.

[156](https://fizyk20.github.io#156)/// The **marker trait** for type-level arrays of type-level numbers.
[157](https://fizyk20.github.io#157)///
[158](https://fizyk20.github.io#158)/// Someday, it may contain an associated constant to produce a runtime array,
[159](https://fizyk20.github.io#159)/// like the other marker traits here. However, that is blocked by [this
[160](https://fizyk20.github.io#160)/// issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/44168).
[161](https://fizyk20.github.io#161)pub trait TypeArray: Sealed {}
[162](https://fizyk20.github.io#162)
[163](https://fizyk20.github.io#163)/// The **marker trait** for type-level numbers which are a power of two.
[164](https://fizyk20.github.io#164)///
[165](https://fizyk20.github.io#165)/// # Examples
[166](https://fizyk20.github.io#166)///
[167](https://fizyk20.github.io#167)/// Here's a working example:
[168](https://fizyk20.github.io#168)///
[169](https://fizyk20.github.io#169)/// ```rust
[170](https://fizyk20.github.io#170)/// use typenum::{PowerOfTwo, P4, P8};
[171](https://fizyk20.github.io#171)///
[172](https://fizyk20.github.io#172)/// fn only_p2<P: PowerOfTwo>() {}
[173](https://fizyk20.github.io#173)///
[174](https://fizyk20.github.io#174)/// only_p2::<P4>();
[175](https://fizyk20.github.io#175)/// only_p2::<P8>();
[176](https://fizyk20.github.io#176)/// ```
[177](https://fizyk20.github.io#177)///
[178](https://fizyk20.github.io#178)/// Numbers which are not a power of two will fail to compile in this example:
[179](https://fizyk20.github.io#179)///
[180](https://fizyk20.github.io#180)/// ```rust,compile_fail
[181](https://fizyk20.github.io#181)/// use typenum::{P9, P511, P1023, PowerOfTwo};
[182](https://fizyk20.github.io#182)///
[183](https://fizyk20.github.io#183)/// fn only_p2<P: PowerOfTwo>() { }
[184](https://fizyk20.github.io#184)///
[185](https://fizyk20.github.io#185)/// only_p2::<P9>();
[186](https://fizyk20.github.io#186)/// only_p2::<P511>();
[187](https://fizyk20.github.io#187)/// only_p2::<P1023>();
[188](https://fizyk20.github.io#188)/// ```
[189](https://fizyk20.github.io#189)pub trait PowerOfTwo: Sealed {}

Struct TArr  Copy item path  Source  `pub struct TArr<V, A> {  }`Expand description `TArr` is a type that acts as an array of types. It is defined similarly to `UInt`, only its
values can be more than bits, and it is designed to act as an array. So you can only add two if
they have the same number of elements, for example.

This array is only really designed to contain `Integer` types. If you use it with others, you
may find it lacking functionality.

# U in typenum::generic_const_mappings - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/generic_const_mappings/type.U.html

Available on

**crate feature**only.`const-generics`## Expand description

The main mapping from a generic `const: usize` to a [ UInt](https://fizyk20.github.io/uint/struct.UInt.html):

[is expected to work like](https://fizyk20.github.io/type.U.html)

`U<N>`[.](https://fizyk20.github.io/consts/type.U42.html)

`UN`- It requires the `const-generics`crate feature to be enabled.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#example)Example

```
use typenum::*;
assert_type_eq!(U<42>, U42);
```
This can even be used in a generic `const N: usize` context, provided the
genericity is guarded by a `where` clause:

```
use typenum::*;
struct MyStruct<const N: usize>;
trait MyTrait { type AssocType; }
impl<const N: usize> MyTrait
    for MyStruct<N>
where
    Const<N> : ToUInt,
{
    type AssocType = U<N>;
}
assert_type_eq!(<MyStruct<42> as MyTrait>::AssocType, U42);
```

---

# typenum::operator_aliases - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/operator_aliases/index.html

## Expand description

Aliases for the type operators used in this crate.
Their purpose is to increase the ergonomics of performing operations on the types defined
here. For even more ergonomics, consider using the `op!` macro instead.

For example, type `X` and type `Y` are the same here:

```
use std::ops::Mul;
use typenum::{Prod, P5, P7};
type X = <P7 as Mul<P5>>::Output;
type Y = Prod<P7, P5>;
assert_type_eq!(X, Y);
```
## Type Aliases[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#types)

- [AbsVal](https://fizyk20.github.io/type.AbsVal.html)
- Alias for the associated type of `Abs`:`AbsVal<A> = <A as Abs>::Output`

# typenum::type_operators - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/type_operators/index.html

## Expand description

Useful **type operators** that are not defined in `core::ops`.

## Traits[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#traits)

- [Abs](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Abs.html)
- A **type operator**that returns the absolute value.
- [Cmp](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Cmp.html)
- A **type operator**for comparing`Self`and`Rhs`. It provides a similar functionality to the function`core::cmp::Ord::cmp`
- [FoldAdd](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.FoldAdd.html)
- A **type operator**that gives the sum of all elements of an`Array`.
- [FoldMul](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.FoldMul.html)
- A **type operator**that gives the product of all elements of an`Array`.
- [Gcd](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Gcd.html)
- A **type operator**that computes the[greatest common divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_common_divisor)of`Self`and`Rhs`.
- [IsEqual](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.IsEqual.html)
- A **type operator**that returns`True`if`Self == Rhs`, otherwise returns`False`.
- [IsGreater](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.IsGreater.html)
- A **type operator**that returns`True`if`Self > Rhs`, otherwise returns`False`.
- [IsGreater](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.IsGreaterOrEqual.html)- OrEqual
- A **type operator**that returns`True`if`Self >= Rhs`, otherwise returns`False`.
- [IsLess](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.IsLess.html)
- A **type operator**that returns`True`if`Self < Rhs`, otherwise returns`False`.
- [IsLess](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.IsLessOrEqual.html)- OrEqual
- A **type operator**that returns`True`if`Self <= Rhs`, otherwise returns`False`.
- [IsNot](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.IsNotEqual.html)- Equal
- A **type operator**that returns`True`if`Self != Rhs`, otherwise returns`False`.
- [Len](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Len.html)
- A **type operator**that gives the length of an`Array`or the number of bits in a`UInt`.
- [Logarithm2](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Logarithm2.html)
- A **type operator**for taking the integer binary logarithm of`Self`.
- [Max](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Max.html)
- A **type operator**that returns the maximum of`Self`and`Rhs`.
- [Min](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Min.html)
- A **type operator**that returns the minimum of`Self`and`Rhs`.
- [Partial](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.PartialDiv.html)- Div
- Division as a partial function. This **type operator**performs division just as`Div`, but is only defined when the result is an integer (i.e. there is no remainder).
- [Pow](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Pow.html)
- A **type operator**that provides exponentiation by repeated squaring.
- [Same](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.Same.html)
- A **type operator**that ensures that`Rhs`is the same as`Self`, it is mainly useful for writing macros that can take arbitrary binary or unary operators.
- [Square](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.SquareRoot.html)- Root
- A **type operator**for taking the integer square root of`Self`.
- [ToInt](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.ToInt.html)
- A **type operator**for taking a concrete integer value from a type.

# typenum::array - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/array/index.html

TArr is a type that acts as an array of types. It is defined similarly to UInt, only its
values can be more than bits, and it is designed to act as an array. So you can only add two if
they have the same number of elements, for example.

Type-level bits.

# typenum::int - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/int/index.html

## Expand description

Type-level signed integers.

Type **operators** implemented:

From `core::ops`: `Add`, `Sub`, `Mul`, `Div`, and `Rem`.
From `typenum`: `Same`, `Cmp`, and `Pow`.

Rather than directly using the structs defined in this module, it is recommended that
you import and use the relevant aliases from the [consts](https://fizyk20.github.io/consts/index.html) module.

Note that operators that work on the underlying structure of the number are
intentionally not implemented. This is because this implementation of signed integers
does *not* use twos-complement, and implementing them would require making arbitrary
choices, causing the results of such operators to be difficult to reason about.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#example)Example

```
use std::ops::{Add, Div, Mul, Rem, Sub};
use typenum::{Integer, N3, P2};
assert_eq!(<N3 as Add<P2>>::Output::to_i32(), -1);
assert_eq!(<N3 as Sub<P2>>::Output::to_i32(), -5);
assert_eq!(<N3 as Mul<P2>>::Output::to_i32(), -6);
assert_eq!(<N3 as Div<P2>>::Output::to_i32(), -1);
assert_eq!(<N3 as Rem<P2>>::Output::to_i32(), -1);
```
## Re-exports[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#reexports)

- `pub use crate::marker_traits::`- [Integer](https://fizyk20.github.io/marker_traits/trait.Integer.html);

---

# typenum::tuple - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/tuple/index.html

## Expand description

[ tuple](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.tuple.html) operations.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#indexing)Indexing

`tuple` types (with up to twelve elements) allow access to values by index, because they implement the [ core::ops::Index](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/index/trait.Index.html) and

[traits:](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/index/trait.IndexMut.html)

`core::ops::IndexMut````
use std::ops::{Index, IndexMut};
use typenum::{U0, U1, U2, U3, Len};
let tuple = ("hello", 5, true);
assert_eq!(tuple[U0::new()], "hello");
assert_eq!(tuple[U1::new()], 5);
assert_eq!(tuple[U2::new()], true);
assert_eq!(tuple.len(), U3::new());
```
Attempting to use an out-of-bounds index is a **compile-time** error.

[ⓘ](https://fizyk20.github.io)

```
use std::ops::{Index, IndexMut};
use typenum::{U0, U1, U2};
let tuple = ("hello", 5, true);
assert_eq!(tuple[U0::new()], "hello"); // OK, the tuple has 3 elements
assert_eq!(tuple[U3::new()], "this is an error!");
```

# typenum::uint - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/uint/index.html

## Expand description

Type-level unsigned integers.

**Type operators** implemented:

From `::core::ops`: `BitAnd`, `BitOr`, `BitXor`, `Shl`, `Shr`, `Add`, `Sub`,
`Mul`, `Div`, and `Rem`.
From `typenum`: `Same`, `Cmp`, and `Pow`.

Rather than directly using the structs defined in this module, it is recommended that
you import and use the relevant aliases from the [consts](https://fizyk20.github.io/consts/index.html) module.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#example)Example

```
use std::ops::{Add, BitAnd, BitOr, BitXor, Div, Mul, Rem, Shl, Shr, Sub};
use typenum::{Unsigned, U1, U2, U3, U4};
assert_eq!(<U3 as BitAnd<U2>>::Output::to_u32(), 2);
assert_eq!(<U3 as BitOr<U4>>::Output::to_u32(), 7);
assert_eq!(<U3 as BitXor<U2>>::Output::to_u32(), 1);
assert_eq!(<U3 as Shl<U1>>::Output::to_u32(), 6);
assert_eq!(<U3 as Shr<U1>>::Output::to_u32(), 1);
assert_eq!(<U3 as Add<U2>>::Output::to_u32(), 5);
assert_eq!(<U3 as Sub<U2>>::Output::to_u32(), 1);
assert_eq!(<U3 as Mul<U2>>::Output::to_u32(), 6);
assert_eq!(<U3 as Div<U2>>::Output::to_u32(), 1);
assert_eq!(<U3 as Rem<U2>>::Output::to_u32(), 1);
```
## Re-exports[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#reexports)

- `pub use crate::marker_traits::`- [PowerOfTwo](https://fizyk20.github.io/marker_traits/trait.PowerOfTwo.html);
- `pub use crate::marker_traits::`- [Unsigned](https://fizyk20.github.io/marker_traits/trait.Unsigned.html);

## Structs[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#structs)

- [UInt](https://fizyk20.github.io/struct.UInt.html)
- `UInt`is defined recursively, where- `B`is the least significant bit and- `U`is the rest of the number. Conceptually,- `U`should be bound by the trait- `Unsigned`and- `B`should be bound by the trait- `Bit`, but enforcing these bounds causes linear instead of logrithmic scaling in some places, so they are left off for now. They may be enforced in future.
- [UTerm](https://fizyk20.github.io/struct.UTerm.html)
- The terminating type for `UInt`; it always comes after the most significant bit.`UTerm`by itself represents zero, which is aliased to`U0`.

## Traits[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#traits)

- [GetBit](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.GetBit.html)
- [SetBit](https://fizyk20.github.io/trait.SetBit.html)
- A **type operator**that, when implemented for unsigned integer`N`, sets the bit at position`I`to`B`.

# cmp in typenum - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/macro.cmp.html

```
macro_rules! cmp {
    ($a:ident < $b:ty) => { ... };
    ($a:ty, < $b:ty) => { ... };
    ($a:ident == $b:ty) => { ... };
    ($a:ty, == $b:ty) => { ... };
    ($a:ident > $b:ty) => { ... };
    ($a:ty, > $b:ty) => { ... };
    ($a:ident <= $b:ty) => { ... };
    ($a:ty, <= $b:ty) => { ... };
    ($a:ident != $b:ty) => { ... };
    ($a:ty, != $b:ty) => { ... };
    ($a:ident >= $b:ty) => { ... };
    ($a:ty, >= $b:ty) => { ... };
}
```
use the `op!` macro instead

## Expand description

A convenience macro for comparing type numbers. Use `op!` instead.

Due to the intricacies of the macro system, if the left-hand operand is more complex than a simple
`ident`, you must place a comma between it and the comparison sign.

For example, you can do `cmp!(P5 > P3)` or `cmp!(typenum::P5, > typenum::P3)` but not
`cmp!(typenum::P5 > typenum::P3)`.

The result of this comparison will always be one of `True` (aka `B1`) or `False` (aka `B0`).

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#example)Example

```
#[macro_use] extern crate typenum;
use typenum::consts::*;
use typenum::Bit;
fn main() {
type Result = cmp!(P9 == op!(P1 + P2 * (P2 - N2)));
assert_eq!(Result::to_bool(), true);
}
```

---

# op in typenum - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/macro.op.html

```
macro_rules! op {
    ($($tail:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Convenient type operations.

Any types representing values must be able to be expressed as `ident`s. That means they need to be
in scope.

For example, `P5` is okay, but `typenum::P5` is not.

You may combine operators arbitrarily, although doing so excessively may require raising the recursion limit.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#example)Example

```
#![recursion_limit="128"]
#[macro_use] extern crate typenum;
use typenum::consts::*;
fn main() {
    assert_type!(
        op!(min((P1 - P2) * (N3 + N7), P5 * (P3 + P4)) == P10)
    );
}
```
Operators are evaluated based on the operator precedence outlined
[here](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference.html#operator-precedence).

The full list of supported operators and functions is as follows:

`*`, `/`, `%`, `+`, `-`, `<<`, `>>`, `&`, `^`, `|`, `==`, `!=`, `<=`, `>=`, `<`, `>`, `cmp`, `sqr`, `sqrt`, `abs`, `cube`, `pow`, `min`, `max`, `log2`, `gcd`

They all expand to type aliases defined in the `operator_aliases` module. Here is an expanded list,
including examples:

Operator `*`. Expands to `Prod`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(P2 * P3), P6);`Operator `/`. Expands to `Quot`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(P6 / P2), P3);`Operator `%`. Expands to `Mod`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(P5 % P3), P2);`Operator `+`. Expands to `Sum`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(P2 + P3), P5);`Operator `-`. Expands to `Diff`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(P2 - P3), N1);`Operator `<<`. Expands to `Shleft`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(U1 << U5), U32);`Operator `>>`. Expands to `Shright`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(U32 >> U5), U1);`Operator `&`. Expands to `And`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(U5 & U3), U1);`Operator `^`. Expands to `Xor`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(U5 ^ U3), U6);`Operator `|`. Expands to `Or`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(U5 | U3), U7);`Operator `==`. Expands to `Eq`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(P5 == P3 + P2), True);`Operator `!=`. Expands to `NotEq`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(P5 != P3 + P2), False);`Operator `<=`. Expands to `LeEq`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(P6 <= P3 + P2), False);`Operator `>=`. Expands to `GrEq`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(P6 >= P3 + P2), True);`Operator `<`. Expands to `Le`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(P4 < P3 + P2), True);`Operator `>`. Expands to `Gr`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(P5 < P3 + P2), False);`Operator `cmp`. Expands to `Compare`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(cmp(P2, P3)), Less);`Operator `sqr`. Expands to `Square`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(sqr(P2)), P4);`Operator `sqrt`. Expands to `Sqrt`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(sqrt(U9)), U3);`Operator `abs`. Expands to `AbsVal`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(abs(N2)), P2);`Operator `cube`. Expands to `Cube`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(cube(P2)), P8);`Operator `pow`. Expands to `Exp`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(pow(P2, P3)), P8);`Operator `min`. Expands to `Minimum`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(min(P2, P3)), P2);`Operator `max`. Expands to `Maximum`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(max(P2, P3)), P3);`Operator `log2`. Expands to `Log2`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(log2(U9)), U3);`Operator `gcd`. Expands to `Gcf`.

`assert_type_eq!(op!(gcd(U9, U21)), U3);`

# tarr in typenum - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/macro.tarr.html

```
macro_rules! tarr {
    () => { ... };
    ($n:ty) => { ... };
    ($n:ty,) => { ... };
    ($n:ty, $($tail:ty),+) => { ... };
    ($n:ty, $($tail:ty),+,) => { ... };
    ($n:ty | $rest:ty) => { ... };
    ($n:ty, $($tail:ty),+ | $rest:ty) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Create a new type-level array. Only usable on Rust 1.13.0 or newer.

There’s not a whole lot you can do with it right now.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#example)Example

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate typenum;
use typenum::consts::*;
type Array = tarr![P3, N4, Z0, P38];
```

# Equal in typenum - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/struct.Equal.html

`pub struct Equal;`## Expand description

A potential output from `Cmp`, this is the type equivalent to the enum variant
`core::cmp::Ordering::Equal`.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#trait-implementations)

# arr.rs - source

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/src/generic_array/arr.rs.html

# generic_array/arr.rs

[1](https://fizyk20.github.io#1)//! Implementation for `arr!` macro.
[2](https://fizyk20.github.io#2)
[3](https://fizyk20.github.io#3)/// Macro allowing for easy construction of Generic Arrays.
[4](https://fizyk20.github.io#4)///
[5](https://fizyk20.github.io#5)/// Type-inference works similarly to `vec![]`
[6](https://fizyk20.github.io#6)///
[7](https://fizyk20.github.io#7)/// **`arr!` can be used in `const` expressions.**
[8](https://fizyk20.github.io#8)///
[9](https://fizyk20.github.io#9)/// Example:
[10](https://fizyk20.github.io#10)/// ```
[11](https://fizyk20.github.io#11)/// # use generic_array::arr;
[12](https://fizyk20.github.io#12)/// use generic_array::typenum::U6;
[13](https://fizyk20.github.io#13)///
[14](https://fizyk20.github.io#14)/// let test = arr![1, 2, 3]; // implicit length
[15](https://fizyk20.github.io#15)/// let test = arr![1; 6];    // explicit length via `Const<N>`
[16](https://fizyk20.github.io#16)/// let test = arr![1; U6];   // explicit length via typenum
[17](https://fizyk20.github.io#17)/// ```
[18](https://fizyk20.github.io#18)///
[19](https://fizyk20.github.io#19)/// # NOTES AND LIMITATIONS
[20](https://fizyk20.github.io#20)/// * As of `generic-array 1.0`, [`From`]/[`from_array`](crate::GenericArray::from_array) can be used directly for a wide range of regular arrays.
[21](https://fizyk20.github.io#21)/// * The `[T; N: ArrayLength]` and `[T; usize]` explicit forms are limited to `Copy` values. Use
[22](https://fizyk20.github.io#22)///   [`GenericArray::generate(|| value.clone())`](crate::GenericSequence::generate) for non-`Copy` items.
[23](https://fizyk20.github.io#23)/// * The `[T; usize]` explicit and `[0, 1, 2, 3]` implicit forms are limited to lengths supported by [`Const<U>`](typenum::Const)
[24](https://fizyk20.github.io#24)#[macro_export]
[25](https://fizyk20.github.io#25)macro_rules! arr {
[26](https://fizyk20.github.io#26)    ($($x:expr),* $(,)*) => ( $crate::GenericArray::from_array([$($x),*]) );
[27](https://fizyk20.github.io#27)    ($x:expr; $N:ty)     => ({
[28](https://fizyk20.github.io#28)        // Bypass `from_array` to allow for any Unsigned array length
[29](https://fizyk20.github.io#29)        const __INPUT_LENGTH: usize = <$N as $crate::typenum::Unsigned>::USIZE;
[30](https://fizyk20.github.io#30)
[31](https://fizyk20.github.io#31)        #[inline(always)]
[32](https://fizyk20.github.io#32)        const fn __do_transmute<T, N: $crate::ArrayLength>(arr: [T; __INPUT_LENGTH]) -> $crate::GenericArray<T, N> {
[33](https://fizyk20.github.io#33)            unsafe { $crate::const_transmute(arr) }
[34](https://fizyk20.github.io#34)        }
[35](https://fizyk20.github.io#35)
[36](https://fizyk20.github.io#36)        __do_transmute::<_, $N>([$x; __INPUT_LENGTH])
[37](https://fizyk20.github.io#37)    });
[38](https://fizyk20.github.io#38)    ($x:expr; $n:expr) => ( $crate::GenericArray::from_array([$x; $n]) );
[39](https://fizyk20.github.io#39)}
[40](https://fizyk20.github.io#40)
[41](https://fizyk20.github.io#41)/// Like [`arr!`], but returns a `Box<GenericArray<T, N>>`
[42](https://fizyk20.github.io#42)///
[43](https://fizyk20.github.io#43)/// Unlike [`arr!`], this is not limited by stack size, only the heap.
[44](https://fizyk20.github.io#44)///
[45](https://fizyk20.github.io#45)/// Example:
[46](https://fizyk20.github.io#46)/// ```
[47](https://fizyk20.github.io#47)/// # use generic_array::{box_arr, typenum::{self, *}};
[48](https://fizyk20.github.io#48)/// // allocate a 16MB Buffer of u128 elements (16 bytes * 10 ^ 6)
[49](https://fizyk20.github.io#49)/// # #[cfg(not(miri))]
[50](https://fizyk20.github.io#50)/// let test = box_arr![1u128; typenum::Exp<U10, U6>];
[51](https://fizyk20.github.io#51)/// //  test: Box<GenericArray<u128, _>>
[52](https://fizyk20.github.io#52)/// ```
[53](https://fizyk20.github.io#53)///
[54](https://fizyk20.github.io#54)/// # NOTES AND LIMITATIONS
[55](https://fizyk20.github.io#55)/// * The `[T; usize]` explicit and `[0, 1, 2, 3]` implicit forms are limited to lengths supported by [`Const<U>`](typenum::Const)
[56](https://fizyk20.github.io#56)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[57](https://fizyk20.github.io#57)#[macro_export]
[58](https://fizyk20.github.io#58)macro_rules! box_arr {
[59](https://fizyk20.github.io#59)    ($($x:expr),* $(,)*) => ({
[60](https://fizyk20.github.io#60)        // deduce length based on a ZST array of units
[61](https://fizyk20.github.io#61)        $crate::GenericArray::__from_vec_helper([$($crate::box_arr_helper!(@unit $x)),*], $crate::alloc::vec![$($x),*])
[62](https://fizyk20.github.io#62)    });
[63](https://fizyk20.github.io#63)    ($x:expr; $N:ty) => ( $crate::GenericArray::<_, $N>::try_from_vec($crate::alloc::vec![$x; <$N as $crate::typenum::Unsigned>::USIZE]).unwrap() );
[64](https://fizyk20.github.io#64)    ($x:expr; $n:expr) => ({
[65](https://fizyk20.github.io#65)        const __LEN: usize = $n;
[66](https://fizyk20.github.io#66)
[67](https://fizyk20.github.io#67)        $crate::GenericArray::<_, <$crate::typenum::Const<__LEN> as $crate::IntoArrayLength>::ArrayLength>::try_from_vec($crate::alloc::vec![$x; __LEN]).unwrap()
[68](https://fizyk20.github.io#68)    });
[69](https://fizyk20.github.io#69)}
[70](https://fizyk20.github.io#70)
[71](https://fizyk20.github.io#71)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[72](https://fizyk20.github.io#72)mod alloc_helper {
[73](https://fizyk20.github.io#73)    use crate::{ArrayLength, GenericArray, IntoArrayLength};
[74](https://fizyk20.github.io#74)
[75](https://fizyk20.github.io#75)    impl<T, N: ArrayLength> GenericArray<T, N> {
[76](https://fizyk20.github.io#76)        #[doc(hidden)]
[77](https://fizyk20.github.io#77)        #[inline(always)]
[78](https://fizyk20.github.io#78)        pub fn __from_vec_helper<const U: usize>(
[79](https://fizyk20.github.io#79)            _empty: [(); U],
[80](https://fizyk20.github.io#80)            vec: alloc::vec::Vec<T>,
[81](https://fizyk20.github.io#81)        ) -> alloc::boxed::Box<GenericArray<T, N>>
[82](https://fizyk20.github.io#82)        where
[83](https://fizyk20.github.io#83)            typenum::Const<U>: IntoArrayLength<ArrayLength = N>,
[84](https://fizyk20.github.io#84)        {
[85](https://fizyk20.github.io#85)            unsafe { GenericArray::try_from_vec(vec).unwrap_unchecked() }
[86](https://fizyk20.github.io#86)        }
[87](https://fizyk20.github.io#87)    }
[88](https://fizyk20.github.io#88)}
[89](https://fizyk20.github.io#89)
[90](https://fizyk20.github.io#90)// TODO: Remove this somehow?
[91](https://fizyk20.github.io#91)#[cfg(feature = "alloc")]
[92](https://fizyk20.github.io#92)#[doc(hidden)]
[93](https://fizyk20.github.io#93)#[macro_export]
[94](https://fizyk20.github.io#94)macro_rules! box_arr_helper {
[95](https://fizyk20.github.io#95)    (@unit $e:expr) => {
[96](https://fizyk20.github.io#96)        ()
[97](https://fizyk20.github.io#97)    };
[98](https://fizyk20.github.io#98)}

# Lsb0 in bitvec::order - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/bitvec/order/struct.Lsb0.html

`pub struct Lsb0;`## Expand description

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#least-significant-first-bit-traversal)Least-Significant-First Bit Traversal

This type orders the bits in an element with the least significant bit first and the most significant bit last, in contiguous order across the element.

The guide has [a chapter](https://bitvecto-rs.github.io/bitvec/memory-representation) with more detailed information on the memory
representation this produces.

This is the default type parameter used throughout the crate. If you do not have a desired memory representation, you should continue to use it, as it provides the best codegen for bit manipulation.

# Cmp in typenum::type_operators - Rust

Source: https://fizyk20.github.io/generic-array/typenum/type_operators/trait.Cmp.html

```
pub trait Cmp<Rhs = Self> {
    type
```
[Output](https://fizyk20.github.io#associatedtype.Output);
}## Expand description

A **type operator** for comparing `Self` and `Rhs`. It provides a similar functionality to
the function
[ core::cmp::Ord::cmp](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html#tymethod.cmp)
but for types.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#example)Example

```
use typenum::{Cmp, Ord, N3, P2, P5};
use std::cmp::Ordering;
assert_eq!(<P2 as Cmp<N3>>::Output::to_ordering(), Ordering::Greater);
assert_eq!(<P2 as Cmp<P2>>::Output::to_ordering(), Ordering::Equal);
assert_eq!(<P2 as Cmp<P5>>::Output::to_ordering(), Ordering::Less);
```
## Required Associated Types[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#required-associated-types)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

[B1](https://fizyk20.github.io/bit/struct.B1.html)>>>,

gcd(x, y) = gcd([max(x, y) - min(x, y)], min(x, y)) if both x and y odd

This will immediately invoke the case for x even and y odd because the difference of two odd numbers is an even number.

pub trait SquareRoot {
    type
```
[Output](https://fizyk20.github.io#associatedtype.Output);
}## Expand description

A **type operator** for taking the integer square root of `Self`.

The integer square root of `n` is the largest integer `m` such
that `n >= m*m`. This definition is equivalent to truncating the
real-valued square root: `floor(real_sqrt(n))`.

`pub trait PowerOfTwo: Sealed { }`## Expand description

The **marker trait** for type-level numbers which are a power of two.

[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#examples)Examples

Here’s a working example:

```
use typenum::{PowerOfTwo, P4, P8};
fn only_p2<P: PowerOfTwo>() {}
only_p2::<P4>();
only_p2::<P8>();
```
Numbers which are not a power of two will fail to compile in this example:

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://fizyk20.github.io#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*
